title: Trump’s Stance on Jensen Huang Is a Tell
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Sometimes a news story is important because it reveals information for the first time
Other times, it’s a big deal because it confirms what many people already suspected
The latest development in the story of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang falls into the second category
As news of Huang’s extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy rocks Silicon Valley, Washington, and Wall Street, President Trump has pleaded ignorance

In particular, he has said he was unaware of the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (no relation) when he traveled to China this past May. “No, I didn’t hear about it then,” he told reporters on Monday

Almost immediately, The New York Times reported that in fact Trump had been warned by Marco Rubio, the national security adviser and secretary of state, while headed to China on Air Force One, just before Jensen Huang boarded the plane for a state visit. (In fact, Trump may have been told even before then: The paper previously reported that Trump was notified about intelligence findings on the relationship last year as well .) The new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, wants to crack down on leaks ; he clearly has his work cut out for him
A few important features of Trump’s approach to the presidency are on display here
First, he has abandoned the pretense of being tough on China, a major talking point during his first presidential run and term
Second, he ignores any intelligence findings that contradict his instincts
Third, this is the latest evidence that, as I wrote last January, Trump does not care about U.S. national security
That doesn’t mean he’s actively hostile to it, or a saboteur; he’s just indifferent to anything but his own interests
In the nearly two years since I first laid out this argument, the president has repeatedly bolstered the case

When Trump was informed that China had infiltrated a tech company that is widely regarded as essential to the health of the global economy as well as a crucial force for maintaining American power and national security—such that the U.S. bans exports of its most powerful chips to China—Trump opted to do nothing and pretend he hadn’t heard
Trump enjoys closeness with titans like Huang and wouldn’t want to endanger that

Huang clearly relished putting Trump on speakerphone during a podcast taping in September. (A serial philanderer himself, Trump said in recent days that Huang “probably has an excuse for” the affair.) The president may have also worried about the risk to the economy of any Nvidia turmoil—both because of the midterm elections and because his own portfolio has grown enormously during the AI boom

Trump was similarly indifferent to the national-security risks of the war in Iran. (Some of his advisers reportedly understood this but did little to dissuade him.) The administration couched the war in terms of eliminating the threat of a nuclear Iran, but given that U.S. intelligence had deemed the program moribund, and given that the Trump administration had claimed to have destroyed the program in 2025, the justification made little sense
And by embarking on a war with no clear strategy or planning, the U.S. has badly depleted its stores of missiles and other munitions, which will spell danger in the event of another conflict

The war has created divisions among American allies and shown that the United States is unable to win a war or guarantee freedom of navigation in the Persian Gulf, all of which weaken its long-term strategic positioning
Not every decision is as consequential as the Iran war, but Trump has repeatedly chosen personal or short-term political gain over American security and national priorities
Accepting the gift of a 747 from Qatar was neither ethical nor a wise security choice—as became clear when Trump had to do his Turkish tarmac turnaround and board a safer plane in August
The president chose his own interests—both flattery and a splashy if minor diesel-fuel deal—in once more embracing Vladimir Putin and distancing himself from Ukraine in October

And as I argued in September , Trump’s decision to treat Venezuela as a vassal state and stifle the popularly supported María Corina Machado is likely to harm American regional interests over time while yielding limited benefits now
To paraphrase Benjamin Franklin , those who would choose some short-term personal benefit over long-term national interest may end up losing both
If Trump hoped that overlooking Huang’s liabilities would prevent turmoil, the bet didn’t pay off
The Wall Street Journal reported this evening that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, after a report late today of another affair , this one with a subordinate
Huang’s behavior has become both a political scandal and an economic liability, after Nvidia’s stock slid over the past few days
What harm this whole incident may have done to national security may not be clear for months or years to come

title: Democrats Should Cut a Deal With Trump
excerpt: On Election Night, Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, described one agenda that congressional Democrats could pu
body: On Election Night, Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, described one agenda that congressional Democrats could pursue over the next two years: investigating the “Trump Crime Family,” as his office put it in a statement
His message was, “Lawyer up.” This tack would be a mistake
The new Democratic majorities should instead take advantage of the fissures now emerging between President Trump and his party to pursue their own legislative goals
Following their electoral wipeout, Republicans are beginning to see Trump as a liability
Trump, for his part, has had little interest in GOP priorities beyond tax cuts, immigration, and Supreme Court appointments, and now is even less wedded to the party’s agenda

During the Republican primaries for president in 2016, Senator Ted Cruz’s pitch to become the party’s nominee was to claim that Trump had no loyalty to the GOP and would cut deals with Democrats whenever it suited him
The Democrats should put this premise to the test

The core terms for such dealmaking are straightforward: Democrats should exploit the whims of the most transactional president in modern American history to secure durable policy gains in areas with broad public support, such as health-care reform (to expand Medicare, reverse cuts to Medicaid, and restore subsidies for the Affordable Care Act), and electoral reform to limit dark money in politics

Deals should also include measures that at least some populist Republicans say they support, such as policies to lower energy costs, cap credit-card interest, and break up monopolies in the health-care sector
Even immigration reform seems to be on the table

To exploit Trump’s awareness that his hard-line approach has hurt him politically, Democrats could offer a deal that appeals to his self-perception as a leader uniquely capable of solving intractable problems
Democrats should convince Trump that promoting these policy priorities will benefit his legacy and burnish his self-image as dealmaker in chief
In exchange, Democrats will need to bank the righteous anger that’s been mounting among leftists for a decade and offer to curb investigations of Trump’s family and close associates
This will not be easy, particularly after the White House counsel’s provocative claim that such investigations would be “a clear abuse of power” and “an affront” to the rule of law
But the opportunities afforded by this moment demand some restraint
The party should also allow the president to build his monuments to himself—the ballroom, the arch, the renovations for that golf course

Trump’s ostentatious, gold-plated aesthetic —classified by some as “dictator chic” —offends many of the taxpayers footing the bill for all this glitz , but his architectural flourishes are largely harmless, and anything he builds can be changed down the road anyway
Democrats would be wiser to focus their efforts on persuading Trump to sign legislation that will outlast him
Chief executives and world leaders have learned how to leverage Trump’s need for adulation to their advantage

Remember those Swiss executives who showed up at the Oval Office last year with a gold Rolex watch and an engraved gold bar and saw their tariff rates plummet a week later? Democrats should do the same: pander to Trump’s ego and avarice, and get something big in return

This has worked before, as evidenced by Trump’s willingness in his first term to work with the Democratic congressional leaders, “ Chuck and Nancy ,” on a budget deal , and his surprising openness to being charmed into partnering with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on building more affordable housing—and it can work again. [ Nick Clegg: Getting too close to Trump was a mistake ] Ironically, working with Trump may even be a way to restore the political norms he has eroded and reverse the Trumpification of the American government

The incoming Congress could pass new disclosure rules, new limits on self-dealing, and whatever guardrails on executive pardons and emergency powers might survive the Supreme Court’s conservative majority
Democrats might entice Trump to sign these reforms by making them take effect in 2029, after he leaves office
One can even imagine Trump relishing the thought that his successors will be bound by norms and rules he openly defied
The most distasteful part of the bargain is the one Trump may value most: that in exchange for these statutes, Democrats won’t seek justice against the president and his family

For lawmakers horrified by the Trump family’s crypto deals and the president’s acceptance of huge gifts from business executives and foreign leaders, such as the luxury jet from the Qatari royal family, this would be a considerable sacrifice
But the trade-off should be clear: On one side is the emotional satisfaction of seeing Trump’s family squirm under questioning from Congress
On the other are transformative and lasting policy reforms
Moreover, congressional Democrats should be realistic about what might even be achieved from the aggressive strategy that Garcia has promised
The Supreme Court has made it difficult to hold Trump accountable personally, and Trump’s Justice Department is unlikely to initiate prosecutions
Trump is almost certain to make liberal use of his pardon powers, and hearings will not claw back the money that Trump and his children have made off the presidency
Voters have already repudiated Trump and his politics
Democrats should translate this anger into the reforms these voters say they want
If Americans come to believe that Democrats accomplished little beyond scoring points for inside-the-Beltway grudges, they may well swing away just in time for the next election
A deal need not mean that Democrats give up on holding anyone accountable for the misdeeds of this administration
Trump is loyal to his family, but he is happy to discard underlings once they stop being useful

The law firms, tech companies, crypto exchanges, and other corporations that participated in or capitulated to Trump’s lawless impulses are all fair game, as are various bit players within the administration

Democrats should stifle their instinct to seek retribution from the top and freely proceed against the rest—as long as this doesn’t detract from the party’s legislative priorities. [ Rachel Maddow: The collapse of America’s most consequential institution ] Getting significant legislation through Congress will be difficult
Even if the Democrats end up with 56 Senate seats, as appears likely, a handful of Republicans will still be needed to overcome a filibuster on substantive legislation
But the electoral thrashing should make some GOP senators more amenable to compromise, especially on matters of affordability and public corruption, both of which had broad support in exit polls

title: Can Republicans Quit Trump?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on how President
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on how President Trump will behave after suffering a humiliating defeat in the 2026 midterms
David warns that the final two years of Trump’s term could be filled with multiple constitutional crises

Then David is joined by Bob Inglis, a former Republican representative, to discuss what it’s like to lose an election, the mindset of the defeated Republicans in 2026, and whether Republicans will do some real soul-searching after being wiped out by a blue wave
Frum and Inglis also talk about the future of faith-based politics in the GOP
Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of the novel All for Nothing by Walter Kempowski, a story of a German family living out the end of the Second World War
The following is a transcript of the episode: Bob Inglis: And I believe that’s what we’re going to see over the next two years
I think that the product is going to be so grotesque that Republicans say, Oh, how did we ever do that? And, Let’s find something new
And it is all about finding that new presentation that is able to say, No, no; we can actually help people, and we won’t just be about power and transactional nature
We’ll be about actually caring for people
David Frum: Welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic

My guest this week is former Republican Congressman Bob Inglis, and we’ll be discussing the experience of defeat and what it does to a person to go through the kind of defeat that so many Republican members of Congress, so many Republican officeholders, have undergone in the past days

This week’s book will be a novel by the German writer Walter Kempowski, All for Nothing, a story of a German family living out the end of the Second World War on its estate in East Prussia and the imminent destruction of the world they knew
But before either the dialogue or the book discussion, some opening thoughts about the world Americans face after the election of 2026

The question that I think will haunt many of us is, given the new political facts in Washington: What is President Trump’s next move? How will President Trump respond to the seeming closing in of the walls and the seeming constraint on his power? Over the past decade, Americans have seen that again and again—when Donald Trump is faced with some form of constraint, he acts out in some way
His power to act out has been reduced, but not eliminated
What might he do? And one of the reasons this is so concerning to me is I think that—I include myself in this—we’ve never had enough imagination of what Donald Trump is capable of

Who thought, as you worried about the second Trump presidency, that roadside executions of peaceful protesters might happen? Who imagined that the United States would find itself on the verge of a war with Denmark or with Canada? These things seem to come out of nowhere, and they came out of constraints on the president’s ego and will
Now, they came at a time when he had the backing of majorities in both houses of Congress, and so a certain amount of impunity

And although one would like to believe that a new Congress and some constraints on his power will make him behave better, in the first presidency—when he lost the House of Representatives in 2018—he behaved worse
He staged his attempted coup against Congress in the overturning of the 2020 election after 2018
He didn’t behave better; he behaved worse

You don’t appoint Stephen Miller as your White House chief of staff if your plan is to work with the Democrats on matters of mutual interest, if you’re going to pursue some kind of immigration deal, or if you’re going to try to balance the budget
Stephen Miller is your choice if your plan is to go to the wall: to refuse subpoenas, to refuse cooperation, to deny information, to fight, fight, fight with everything you have
There are resources that remain at the president’s disposal
He still has considerable unilateral tariff power
He has, of course, his powers of war and peace
He still controls ICE and can deploy that force at his command
And while Congress has the power of the purse, the president can even weaponize that against Congress
We are approaching in the spring of 2027, once again, the ritual of the renewal of the lifting of the debt ceiling

The United States has this strange practice where Congress votes the spending, Congress votes the taxes, and, if there’s a gap that must be covered by borrowing, Congress has to vote again to allow the borrowing to happen

This has often been a pretty automatic process, but again and again in the past 20 years, especially when Republicans have control of one or both houses of Congress, we’ve seen attempts to weaponize the debt ceiling—to say to the president, for Congress to say to the president, especially when there’s a Republican majority, We won’t raise the debt ceiling with all the catastrophic consequences that will follow, unless you do this or that
What we’ve not seen is a president try to weaponize the debt ceiling and say, I won’t sign a raising of the debt ceiling unless you do this or that for me
This is a different kind of president who’s capable of weaponizing anything, including the tools that previous Republican Congresses have used against Democratic presidents
There’s no inherent reason why it couldn’t go the other way around
We might see President Trump abuse powers of war and peace, or powers of flows of information, to give Putin more, to give the Chinese more
We might see President Trump absolutely go on the rampage against Congress, even trying to extend the methods used against Ilhan Omar
But that technique, once pioneered against Omar, might be used against other people, too
Could you imagine a dozen investigations, a dozen attempted indictments against members of Congress whom Donald Trump doesn’t like? Kash Patel still leads the FBI
Congress cannot impeach everybody, and it certainly can’t remove everybody

title: The Atlantic Announces Amanda Mull, Annalisa Quinn, and Erik Slavin as Staff Writers
excerpt: As part of its continued newsroom growth, The Atlantic is announcing the return of Amanda Mull as a staff writer; the hires of Annalisa Quinn and Erik Slavin as
body: As part of its continued newsroom growth, The Atlantic is announcing the return of Amanda Mull as a staff writer; the hires of Annalisa Quinn and Erik Slavin as staff writers; and the hire of Bill Tipper as a senior editor overseeing the creation and launch of The Atlantic Book Club, coming in 2027
This is a homecoming for Amanda, who was a staff writer at The Atlantic from 2018 to 2024, writing countless memorable pieces on culture, trends, fashion, and the way we live

Annalisa joins from The Boston Globe , where most recently she was the deputy editor of the Globe’s Sunday magazine, and this year wrote what’s been hailed as “The Greatest Article That Has Ever Been Written” (per The Daily Beast ) about easing mask policies at a lesbian bar

Erik is joining The Atlantic ’s Pentagon team; he was the editor in chief of Stars and Stripes and spent more than two decades at the publication, before being fired by the Defense Department this summer after he refused to bend to the department’s censorship demands
Bill is joining as a senior editor overseeing the creation and launch of The Atlantic Book Club in 2027
He was most recently an editor at The Wall Street Journal , where he produced a weekly newsletter and edited a wide variety of stories for the Journal
Below are the staff announcements from editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg: Amanda Mull is returning as a staff writer

Ever since that tragic day in 2024 when Amanda Mull left for her Bloombergian rumspringa , we’ve been on the hunt for someone who could replace her, someone with an acute eye, a gift for language, a deep feeling for humans and their foibles, a cockeyed sense of humor and that ineffable Mullish spark

We looked for someone who understood the weird ways of American consumerism, someone who would be willing to turn herself into a test rabbit for a set of absurd Goop products, a reporter who could explain why sweaters are bad now, why ballet flats have always been bad, why self-checkout is a failed experiment
A person who could explore obsessional behavior toward diamonds and Herm è s , and who also knew which flour to use to make the best biscuits
What became known as the “Amanda Mull slot,” we learned, was impossible to fill
No matter how hard we tried, no one quite fit the bill
We have finally discovered someone who could replace Amanda Mull, and that person is … Amanda Mull
We are thrilled to let you know that Amanda has rediscovered the One True Path, and will be joining us again at The Atlantic
Annalisa Quinn is joining us as a staff writer
For the last several years, Annalisa has been writing and editing for The Boston Globe , where most recently she has served as deputy editor of the Globe ’s Sunday magazine

You are all no doubt familiar with her work, including “The Greatest Article That Has Ever Been Written” (per The Daily Beast ), a mega-viral piece about the contretemps over the masking policy at a now-immortal lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts

But her name should have been familiar to you long before that, because she’s been producing first-rate journalism and literary essays for years, at The Financial Times and as a Berlin-based freelancer for The New York Times , among other places
She also served for a decade as a literary critic for NPR

She has a capacious range, bringing empathy and intelligence to her writing about homelessness and addiction; Elvis impersonators; the researchers trying to piece together the Stasi archives; and, of course, books
Erik Slavin is coming aboard as a staff writer, joining our stellar Pentagon team
Erik is one of the most experienced and gifted defense correspondents and editors in the country
As all of you know, the Defense Department fired Erik in August after he refused to bend to the department’s censorship demands

As he wrote for us not long after, “I was fired after I said in an appearance on CBS News that my personal red line would be if the Pentagon ever instructed me not to publish a perfectly accurate story

It is telling that I am being fired for describing the most anodyne of journalistic ethics, a position that any self-respecting reporter in any free society would hold, and that the Pentagon interpreted as insubordination.” I am very pleased that The Atlantic will provide a home for Erik’s coverage of the Pentagon, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and the armed services
Like Stars and Stripes itself, Erik is known for his deep and knowledgeable coverage of the lives of America’s men and women in uniform
This is an important and generally under-covered subject
Erik joined Stars and Stripes in 2005, and has reported from Iraq, South Korea, and Japan, where he led coverage of the Great East Japan earthquake and nuclear disaster
From 2017 to 2025, he served as the newspaper’s bureau chief for Europe and the Middle East, overseeing coverage of Afghanistan, NATO, and Ukraine
He moved to Washington to become the editor in chief of Stars and Stripes in 2025
Earlier in his career, he reported from Capitol Hill and worked as a reporter and editor in Florida
Bill Tipper is coming onboard as a senior editor overseeing the creation and launch of The Atlantic Book Club
Building a truly original subscriber experience requires hiring a unicorn, and that’s what Bill is
After getting his Ph.D. in English, Bill left academia for the wild world of the Books Internet
At BN.com, he helped launch the Barnes & Noble Review , an independent hub for some of the best online writing about books

Years ahead of most outlets, he saw the potential for new ways to connect with people who love literature, launching an author-interview podcast and an ambitious read-along series devoted to Stephen King’s complete works
More recently, as an editor at The Wall Street Journal , he has produced a weekly newsletter and edited a wide variety of stories with exceptional rigor and foresight
Bill is widely known in the literary world for his intelligence, kindness, and energy, and we’re delighted that he has agreed to take on a project that will enrich The Atlantic for years to come

title: Modi Is Facing ‘A Million Mutinies’
excerpt: F or more than a decade, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has relied on fear to throttle dissent in India
body: F or more than a decade, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has relied on fear to throttle dissent in India
It has jailed protesters, deployed a pliant media to vilify critics, and fanned the flames of communal violence
This year, that playbook appears to have lost its efficacy
Discontent has grown, and Modi’s power no longer seems unassailable
The first signs of this change emerged over the summer
Tens of thousands of young people thronged Delhi to demand that India’s education minister resign
They had come of age in a country where public education was crumbling, economic growth favored the rich, and jobs were scarce
They had little patience for news channels perceived to be government mouthpieces—they even heckled several reporters out of their demonstrations
The summer’s young demonstrators mounted posters and circulated cheeky memes and slogans that took direct aim at the prime minister
When police attacked one of their marches with pellet guns, tear gas, and shock batons , the violence stoked public indignation that swelled the movement’s ranks

Modi then tried to endear himself with the digital-age protesters: He implored them to stand down in an Instagram selfie video, and his colleagues from the Hindu-nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party delivered speeches peppered with youthful slang, such as delulu and clock it
These efforts just earned the BJP more mockery
The police have used force against protesters before, but the effects were very different
In 2019, the BJP championed a discriminatory citizenship law; demonstrations erupted, and the police used brutal means to crush them, including abetting and even participating in communal violence
The following year, the government announced sweeping agricultural reforms
Farmers who protested that these favored giant corporations faced a violent crackdown
In neither case was the popular outrage as widespread as it was this summer

That is likely because those past protests were associated with the Sikh and Muslim communities, which the BJP and its supporters had effectively maligned, playing into and deepening long-standing prejudices. [ Read: Why India is erupting ] By contrast, this summer, many of those demanding the education minister’s resignation came from privileged Hindu families—the very constituents that the prime minister and his party count on for support
The government therefore couldn’t target them with as heavy a hand
The movement culminated in the education minister’s ouster
Right-wing provocateurs and media outlets—aided, in several instances, by police officials and BJP supporters and politicians—singled out Muslim , female , and queer protesters for retaliation
This fall saw the development of a new protest movement in the capital, centering on the denial of a fundamental democratic promise: the right to vote
Since 2025, millions of names have been struck from India’s voter rolls in a revision process that has raised many questions

At stake, Anjali Bhardwaj, an activist, told me, “is the very soul of India’s electoral democracy.” Those agitating against the assault on the franchise repurposed some of the same rallying cries from the summer protests—for instance, “ Jab Jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai ,” or, “Whenever Modi feels the heat, he sends the police onto the streets.” And the government again turned to repression
Security forces detained thousands of people carrying out flash protests, beating many and confronting others with legal charges
But many citizens now see these tactics less as a show of strength than as an admission of fear
The new movement has not been extinguished, and opposition political parties have come out to show their support
At the same time, other, mostly unrelated protests have erupted or continued in different parts of the country
Since January, workers in at least 10 states have staged a reported 275 strikes

In October alone, tribal residents from a village in Madhya Pradesh lay on mock funeral pyres to protest an $87 billion river-linking project that has displaced them; scores of protesters in Mumbai demanded accountability from a public university over allegations that a student who died by suicide faced caste discrimination there; and students at another public university, in Delhi, successfully agitated for the restoration of a long-defunct students’ union
In Arunachal Pradesh, protesters are resisting a mega-dam project that they say will submerge more than two dozen villages

All of these demonstrations have been met with major police pressure, much of it violent, and persisted in spite of it. “A million mutinies are now finally coming to the fore,” Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told me

Intimidating opposition members—“labeling people anti-national, anti-development, all that”—once worked to undermine such movements’ confidence, Donthi said. “That is not working now.” The government has yet to recover from the blow that the summer protests dealt its image, according to Neha, the national president of the left-affiliated All India Students’ Association. (Neha goes by only their first name and uses they/them pronouns.) “The young people who have been part of these protests don’t really believe in the invincible aura of the prime minister at all,” Neha told me. “If anything, he has been acting as a wonderful source of memes and jokes and satire, and that has been the extent of his contribution to the young generation.” T his fall’s protest movement has its roots in an administrative process that began more than a year ago
In June 2025, just before contentious assembly elections in several states, India’s election commission announced that it would revise the country’s voter rolls
India has a process for this, called an Intensive Revision, and it has been done eight times in the past
But this Special Intensive Revision (as it was called) was different
The process was hurried and lacked transparency
Unlike past revisions , the SIR shrank the electorate, and not by a little: It struck 130 million names from the rolls
Many of those deleted had died, moved to another constituency, were registered to multiple polling stations, or could not be found by enumerators
But the effects of the revision could not be explained solely by such cases

title: The Stealth Friendship Killer
excerpt: Scientists have identified the three leading killers of mom-friend plans: the never-ending day-care virus, the sitter who bailed, and the mysterious vortex that
body: Scientists have identified the three leading killers of mom-friend plans: the never-ending day-care virus, the sitter who bailed, and the mysterious vortex that is “out of town.” The first two are unavoidable, but the third is a choice that society, collectively, seems to be making more and more
Out of town is where all of your friends are when you’ve finally decided to host a playdate
Out of town is where everyone is for the entirety of August
Want to grab a drink? I would love to, but I am, well, you get it
We don’t know whether Americans are actually making more weekend trips; the most recent large-scale, comprehensive assessment on the topic was conducted in 1995

The most common reasons that Americans gave last year for not spending more time with their friends were their own mental-health issues, not having enough money, and being too busy ; travel didn’t appear anywhere in the top six
And going away is not an entirely bad thing
Hall, a University of Kansas communication professor who studies friendship, told me that he encourages people to visit out-of-town friends to keep those relationships alive
But something is going on here, especially among better-off Americans, and it can make building community challenging
If people are always going away, they can’t be around for preplanned meetups or be run into casually, interactions that are the glue holding together friendship and social life

As the anonymous writer behind the Substack Cartoons Hate Her wrote in 2024, people say they want “a village” where they currently live, but they nevertheless spend a suspicious amount of time going “out of town.” (She put the term in scare quotes, as though the Catskills were a newly discovered bacteria.) When she hosted a party for her son’s preschool class, for example, only about a third of the kids showed up—“surprise, everyone else was ‘out of town,’” she wrote

In a discussion of the article on the DC Urban Moms and Dads message board, a poster wrote, “I don’t know why my neighbors are always out of town on weekends,” before adding that, as a consequence, he or she also travels frequently, and thus contributes to the weekend desertion of the neighborhood

Elsewhere on the internet, the “out of town” phenomenon is a recurring grievance wherever women, people over 30, and particularly women over 30 gather. [ Read: The friendship paradox ] Several demographic trends help explain why so few people ever seem to be home on the weekends

Americans have been prioritizing vacations over the past 20 years, even as the cost of living has increased, according to preliminary data gathered by Jeffrey LaMondia, a civil-engineering professor at Auburn University who studies American travel habits

His research subjects, he told me, “were rearranging their annual budgets to make sure that they had funds to take these trips.” A 2016 study by LaMondia and two colleagues also found that people who have higher incomes and who live in denser areas near airports are more likely to travel for fun
This same demographic is likelier to do remote work, which in some cases requires people to drive or fly into headquarters periodically to check in

Many people combine these work trips with a vacation day or two, a practice known by the ungainly name “ bleisure .” What’s more, highly educated people have been moving farther away from their families of origin in recent decades, which means that seeing relatives or childhood friends might necessitate a weekend trip

Because people are so geographically spread out, even a modest wedding or baby shower might require high-school friends, college roommates, and extended-family members to all fly in from different cities
And don’t get me started on the rise of kids’ travel sports
An acquaintance of mine recently tried to get a bunch of us neighbors together to go to a bar for one (one!) drink
The week of, several people canceled because their kids had out-of-town sports competitions the morning after the gathering
It’s not like I’m some country mouse who barely leaves my home
For several years before we became parents, my husband and I lived in Northern Virginia but spent much of the winter in Florida
We, too, would gripe about our village-less-ness and then promptly book a month-long Airbnb in Miami
While we were away, we missed countless house parties, museum outings, and other events with our friends in Washington, D.C
I even missed a book talk by a friend whose book I loved and whom I never get to see
Part of what makes this topic so difficult to talk about is that many of the reasons people travel are good ones

Who would shame someone for attending their kid’s soccer game or their cousin’s wedding? But when weekends away add up, people are not truly living in the actual village that they want to be their “village.” “If you invest entirely in the people who are not there,” said Hall—who, again, generally supports the idea of people traveling—“then you’re missing out on building relationships with people who are in your geographical same location.” This is why remote work can feel so—remote

You’re not truly relating to either your virtual co-workers or your physical neighbors. [ Read: Fold laundry with me! ] In The Death and Life of Great American Cities , Jane Jacobs wrote that “the trust of a city street is formed over time from many, many little public sidewalk contacts.” This being 1961, she offered the example of someone “getting advice from the grocer and giving advice to the newsstand man” or “hearing about a job from the hardware man.” This picture, although too rosy and now outdated, still holds true in some respects: People tend to befriend the folks they run into regularly over time—which can occur through planned hangouts but also happenstance, in the school pickup line or while waiting for their coffee at a neighborhood café

When people travel frequently, they may miss out on encounters that can lead to connection. “If you have an erratic schedule where instead of going to the laundry every Sunday afternoon, you just go randomly when you run out of clothes, the laundromat’s not going to be a fertile place to find friends,” Rebecca Adams, a professor emeritus of sociology and gerontology at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, told me
Repeated encounters matter because they help make our friendships smoother and less awkward

The more you see someone, the better you get to know them, and “greater familiarity reduces your social energy costs,” Hall said. “You don’t have to worry about what another person thinks of you.” You can break out of small talk and get straight to the juicy drama because you’re not filling the person in on what you’re like—they already know because they’ve been around to find out
I’m certain that as soon as this article is published, I’ll be caught red-handed at the airport, 400 pounds of baby-travel gear in tow
I still travel! I’m sure that many other people I know will continue to as well
But lately I’ve become less interested in going out of town just to add variety to my weekends
The place I live already has plenty of things to do and people to see—as long as I’m around to see them.

title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
excerpt: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming thresh
body: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming threshold the Paris Agreement was designed to prevent
The money problem: Rich nations promised $300 billion a year by 2035 for climate action, but delivered less than half that in 2024

Fossil fuels back in the spotlight: After last year's final agreement didn't mention "fossil fuels" once, expect a fight over language—especially with cohosts Australia and Turkey both deeply tied to coal and gas. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148308" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey
COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world
Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20
This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis
And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular

Here’s what you should know about COP31.   In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked
This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US
President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change

That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.  Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels

In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming

There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.  Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas
The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage
The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country)
Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels
Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them
But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once

This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal
Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching

These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.   One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go
The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there
The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use
Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity
Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest
Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions

The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.  With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change
I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.  To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death
Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud
Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine
Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands
MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits
Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk
Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify
The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models
Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology
The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts
Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking Only around a dozen nations are reportedly ready to sign it. ( Politico ) + It requires quadrupling the pace of electrification. ( New Scientist $) + John Kerry says the US must follow China on clean energy. ( Guardian ) + But the US skipped the talks entirely for a second year. ( NYT $) + What’s the future of electricity? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 The Nvidia spy scandal reportedly involves $7.5 billion of chips Alice Huang allegedly obtained 240,000 restricted chips. ( Information $) + Trump was told of Huang’s spy link on Air Force One . ( NYT $) + Experts warn the scandal could erode America’s AI lead. ( Verge ) + Nvidia’s slide has let Microsoft overtake it in value. ( Reuters $) 3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible” Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. ( NYT $) + This is why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Anthropic has scaled back its IPO valuation to $1.4 trillion It aimed for $2 trillion before the recent AI jitters. ( Guardian ) 5 Drone strikes have wiped out 3% of Yandex’s cloud customer data Ukraine hit three of its data centers in October. ( Reuters $) + Ukraine’s drones are fighting data centers for fiber. ( Ars Technica ) 6 Moderna says its new vaccine could prevent cancer in high-risk people The company’s CEO calls it the “holy grail” of cancer prevention. ( FT $) + Hong Kong is testing a next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment. ( SCMP ) 7 Scientists have slowly reversed human cells’ ages by decades One age marker was set back as far as 60 years. ( Wired $) + “Reprogramming” is the buzziest de-aging idea. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 Robot vessels are hunting for mines in the Strait of Hormuz AI helps them spot mines camouflaged on the seabed. ( BBC ) 9 Life may have started inside a tiny bubble That’s the idea behind the “lipid first” origin theory. ( Quanta ) 10 As Voyager 1 reaches a light day from Earth, here’s what it’s taught us Its discoveries rewrote textbooks in real time. ( New Scientist $) Quote of the day “What a dereliction of duty

He’s supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends.” —Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy
One more thing How refrigeration ruined fresh food Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit
It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity
And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus
According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system

Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.  Read the full story on her research . —Allison Arieff We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A whisky made like wine is wowing the spirits world. + Britain lost in the fog makes for hauntingly beautiful photos . + Chronophoto is a fiendishly addictive game that challenges you to date old photos to the year. + Dozens of saxophonists met up in New York to play the gloriously cheesy riff from George Michael’s “Careless Whisper.”

title: El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nations
url:
<title>El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nations</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771390/original/file-20261111-64-h9zgjd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C82%2C4765%2C3176&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A Salvadoran Army soldier stands guard at a camp in Port-au-Prince,  Haiti, on Oct. 31, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/salvadoran-army-soldier-stands-guard-at-their-encampment-in-news-photo/2302416797?phrase=Haiti%20Salvador&amp;adppopup=true">Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>On Nov. 10, 2026, El Salvador President Nayib Bukele <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/10/salvadoran-troops-target-haitian-gang-leaving-20-dead">posted footage</a> of attack helicopters firing on a compound near Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince. </p>

<p>He had earlier <a href="https://www.infobae.com/america/agencias/2026/11/10/la-casa-del-lider-de-la-pandilla-haitiana-400-mawozo-fue-destruida-segun-afirma-bukele/">requested, via a social media post in Haitian Creole, the address</a> of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, one of Haiti’s most powerful criminal organizations. Bukele subsequently claimed the operation, conducted with Haitian police, had <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmvg2xdwnwezo">demolished Joseph’s residence</a> and gang headquarters. As many as <a href="https://www.aol.com/articles/haiti-police-salvadoran-troops-destroy-161358000.html">20 people were killed</a>, although Joseph was reportedly absent.</p>

<p>The attack comes amid a flurry of anti-gang operations in Haiti. On Nov. 6, Mathias Saintil, head of the “Boston” gang in Cité Soleil, <a href="https://ca.marketscreener.com/news/haiti-pm-says-gang-leader-mathias-saintil-dead-ce785fd2df89f527">was killed</a> in a drone strike by a Haitian special task force, prompting Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé <a href="https://x.com/citoyendidier/status/2118853047925551366">to declare on the social media platform X</a> “one less gang leader.” Erik Prince, founder of the private military firm Vectus Global, <a href="https://beta.lenouvelliste.com/article/273679/le-premier-ministre-fils-aime-annonce-la-mort-de-mathias-saintil-lun-des-chefs-de-gangs-de-viv-ansanm">responded</a>: “Nice shot.”</p>

<p>As an expert on <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oSuc5tUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">organized crime in Latin America and the Caribbean</a>, I believe these operations mark both a dramatic escalation in Haiti’s fight against organized crime and the first overseas test of Bukele’s security model. The intervention is <a href="https://apnews.com/article/dominican-republic-abinader-salvador-haiti-gangs-troops-55c1bdb8c82fce3b5d49ad33e6d8c194">drawing support</a> from some regional leaders and pro-Bukele networks, even as concerns grow over civilian casualties and whether military gains can translate into lasting security.</p>

<h2>Rescue mission or military offensive?</h2>

<p>El Salvador already had a limited presence in Haiti as <a href="https://press.un.org/en/2026/sc16482.doc.htm">one of six countries</a> contributing personnel to the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force, or GSF. The force was <a href="https://docs.un.org/en/S/RES/2793(2025)">authorized in 2025</a> to help Haitian authorities reclaim cities and streets from violent gangs that control swathes of the impoverished nation. But it remains <a href="https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10860194">severely understaffed</a> and has struggled to translate military operations into lasting territorial gains.</p>

<p>Then, in an Oct. 18 gang ambush, four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the Gang Suppression Force <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/four-salvadoran-air-force-members-missing-after-gang-ambush-haiti-2026-10-19/">disappeared</a>. Their burned vehicle <a href="https://apnews.com/article/haiti-el-salvador-gangs-bukele-0302160e058789506d72c9e2a6c1bfc9">was recovered</a>, but their fate remains uncertain. </p>

<p>Either way, Bukele used the incident to justify expanding El Salvador’s military presence in Haiti. Within weeks he had <a href="https://apnews.com/article/haiti-gangs-el-salvador-bukele-filsaime-c0986699cb1d618aed28f406d5a6975d">sent roughly 2,500 troops</a>, along with armored vehicles and attack helicopters, in what he <a href="https://www.local10.com/news/world/2026/10/21/bukele-says-military-operation-launched-to-rescue-salvadorans-held-by-gangs-in-haiti/">initially called</a> a rescue mission. </p>

<p>They joined an already crowded battlefield. Haiti’s <a href="https://www.unmissions.org/en/unsoh/news/security-council-extends-gang-suppression-force-and-unsoh-mandates">police and army operate alongside the GSF</a>, authorized but not commanded by the United Nations. The Haitian task force involved in operations against Saintil also works with former Blackwater CEO Prince’s <a href="https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-officials-see-closer-ties-with-trump-ally-princes-security-firm-in-haiti-military-adviser-says-4804441">Vectus Global</a>, while vigilante groups patrol contested neighborhoods. Dozens of armed gangs associated with the gang coalition <a href="https://main.un.org/securitycouncil/en/content/viv-ansanm">Viv Ansanm</a> control large parts of Port-au-Prince and operate beyond the capital.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A vehicle with GSF written on it is loaded with men." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=387&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=387&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=387&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=487&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=487&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771391/original/file-20261111-64-7wow9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=487&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Special forces from El Salvador ride in a Gang Suppression Force truck in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Oct 23, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/special-forces-from-el-salvador-ride-in-a-gang-suppression-news-photo/2301188572?phrase=Haiti%20Salvador&amp;adppopup=true">Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The Gang Suppression Force was authorized by the U.N. Security Council to <a href="https://apnews.com/article/haiti-gangs-salvador-attack-military-dd5d4b617fc526d3f7d994274732fc7e">deploy up to 5,550 personnel</a>, and it currently has roughly 2,000 on the ground. Most of the Salvadoran troops now in Haiti operate <a href="https://lenouvelliste.com/en/article/273523/un-the-vast-majority-of-salvadoran-troops-do-not-fall-under-the-frg">outside its command</a>. Haitian Prime Minister Fils-Aimé <a href="https://apnews.com/article/fefbf2e40c1eef1cac6b0281cef961d0">insists that Haiti directs</a> the operations. Yet neither government has publicly disclosed the agreement specifying Salvadoran authority, rules of engagement or the deployment’s duration.</p>

<p>Without a <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/11/haiti-los-gobiernos-de-haiti-y-el-salvador-deben-garantizar-que-el-despliegue-militar-salvadoreno-respete-los-derechos-humanos/">published deployment agreement</a>, the chain of command and rules for authorizing strikes remain unclear to the public. </p>

<p>Despite President Donald Trump’s support for Bukele, Secretary of State Marco Rubio <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/11/secretary-of-state-marco-rubio-remarks-to-the-press-21/">has distanced Washington</a> from the Salvadoran offensive, saying the U.S. was “not actively involved.” He <a href="https://www.axios.com/2026/11/10/el-salvador-state-department-haiti-gangs">warned</a> that poor coordination could lead to friendly fire, while U.S. diplomats <a href="https://www.axios.com/2026/11/10/el-salvador-state-department-haiti-gangs">formally protested</a> the risks to multinational troops and civilian personnel.</p>

<p>Salvadoran authorities <a href="https://www.axios.com/2026/11/10/el-salvador-state-department-haiti-gangs">dispute American allegations</a> that their gunfire struck the U.S. embassy and endangered multinational troops. They also <a href="https://www.axios.com/2026/11/10/el-salvador-state-department-haiti-gangs">questioned the credibility</a> of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti. </p>

<h2>Uncertain rules of engagement</h2>

<p>Haiti’s security crisis is dire. </p>

<p>In recent years, organized violence has reached levels associated with armed conflict. Almost <a href="https://binuh.unmissions.org/en/binuh/communiques-de-presse/haiti-la-situation-des-droits-humains-reste-extremement-preoccupante-au">6,000 people</a> were killed in 2025, and <a href="https://efe.com/mundo/haiti-violencia-muertos-crisis-seguridad-tercer-trimestre-2026/">more than 4,000</a> in the first nine months of 2026. Nearly <a href="https://dtm.iom.int/reports/haiti-report-internal-displacement-situation-round-14-august-2026">1.5 million Haitians have been displaced</a> as of August 2026, and expanded offensives and gang reprisals could drive more from their homes. </p>

<p>An independent <a href="https://warwatch.ch/situations/non-international-armed-conflict-in-haiti/classification/">legal assessment</a> by the Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights classifies fighting between Haitian forces and the Viv Ansanm coalition as a noninternational armed conflict, a legal category that includes civil wars. The International Committee of the Red Cross has separately <a href="https://www.icrc.org/en/article/haiti-do-everything-possible-protect-population-effects-escalating-armed-violence">warned of the risks to civilians</a>, urging all sides to respect international law. </p>

<p>The distinction matters because the rules on lethal force are different in war and policing. Both require civilians to be protected. But in an armed conflict, members of armed groups with combat roles can be targeted even when they pose no immediate threat. In a police operation, simply being suspected of gang membership is not enough to justify killing someone – lethal force is generally allowed only when necessary to protect lives.</p>

<p>Of particular concern is the growing use of explosive drones and helicopter attacks in residential areas. At least <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/03/10/haiti-drone-strikes-put-residents-at-risk">1,243 people were killed in 141 drone operations</a> between March 2025 and January 2026, including at least 60 people reportedly unconnected to gangs, 17 of them children. These operations predated the Salvadoran escalation but demonstrate the risks of using explosive weapons in populated areas.</p>

<p>At the same time, overlapping mandates for foreign troops and private military contractors could complicate investigations into civilian casualties and allegations of unlawful attacks.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Exporting the Bukele model</h2>

<p>Some Haitians, exhausted by insecurity, welcome the international intervention. </p>

<p>Crowds have <a href="https://efe.com/mundo/2026-11-07/marchas-apoyo-bukele-haiti/">cheered Salvadoran soldiers</a>, waving sticks and chanting Bukele’s name. A prominent Haitian human rights advocate <a href="https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/around-1000-soldiers-from-el-salvador-have-deployed-to-haiti-source-says-4976576">supported the deployment</a> while warning that residents of gang-controlled neighborhoods are not necessarily gang members.</p>

<p>Bukele promotes the offensive through <a href="https://apnews.com/article/nayib-bukele-el-salvador-haiti-elections-war-on-gangs-un-rubio-democracy-5c8a5e284835778c31c9ff78c140afcd">videos of troops and airstrikes</a> amplified by Salvadoran officials and pro-government influencers. Messages in Haitian Creole and Spanish that <a href="https://www.laprensani.com/2026/11/10/internacionales/3810551-bukele-destruye-cuartel-pandillas-haiti">portray the strikes</a> as victories against gangs closely resemble the government’s widely circulated footage of mass arrests and prison transfers in El Salvador.</p>

<p>Under Bukele, who came to power in 2019, <a href="https://abc3340.com/news/nation-world/el-salvador-turnaround-from-murder-capital-to-safe-haven-nayib-bukele-cecot">homicides in El Salvador have plummeted</a>, <a href="https://www.project-syndicate.org/magazine/bukele-effect-in-latin-america-risks-to-replicating-el-salvador-model-by-robert-muggah-2026-03">boosting a belief</a> in parts of South America and the Caribbean that an iron fist approach to gang violence is worth the associated cost to human rights. Indeed, security hardliners across Latin America have <a href="https://english.elpais.com/international/2023-03-17/bukele-intensifies-war-on-gangs-2000-more-inmates-transferred-to-biggest-prison-in-all-america.html?outputType=amp&amp;utm">pointed to</a> El Salvador’s falling homicide rate to justify similar crackdowns. Dominican President Luis Abinader has <a href="https://apnews.com/article/dominican-republic-abinader-salvador-haiti-gangs-troops-55c1bdb8c82fce3b5d49ad33e6d8c194">endorsed the intervention</a> and confirmed logistical and intelligence cooperation.</p>

<p>Yet the Salvadoran model has relied on emergency powers and mass incarceration. Around <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/10/07/el-salvador-mass-trials-a-mockery-of-justice">1.7% of Salvadorans are imprisoned</a> – by far <a href="https://www.prisonstudies.org/world-prison-data/highest-lowest/highest-lowest-prison-population-rate?language_content_entity=en-gb">the highest rate in the world</a>.</p>

<p>Haiti presents greater operational challenges. According to the U.N. Office for Drugs and Crime, gangs hold extensive territory, <a href="https://www.unodc.org/unodc/frontpage/2024/April/haiti_-gangs-have-more-firepower-than-the-police.html">possess heavy weapons</a> and maintain connections to political and commercial networks. Haitian institutions are weaker, and <a href="https://childrenandarmedconflict.un.org/en/news/special-representative-secretary-general-children-and-armed-conflict-concludes-first-visit">children are widely recruited</a> into armed groups from a young age. Sustaining territorial gains would require functioning police and courts, along with protection for residents after foreign troops leave.</p>

<p>The expanded Salvadoran presence in Haiti also carries political risks for both governments. Bukele is <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/el-salvador-presidents-party-nominates-bukele-seek-third-term-2026-07-13/">seeking a third term</a> in February 2027, following <a href="https://www.asamblea.gob.sv/node/13645">constitutional changes</a> that removed presidential term limits. </p>

<p>Salvadoran military casualties could stir criticism at home and pressure him to escalate, particularly with the <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/salvadoran-technicians-missing-haiti-gang-ambush-601077">four Salvadoran technicians</a> whose disappearance prompted the rescue mission still missing. For his part in Haiti, Fils-Aimé has publicly backed the offensive ahead of Haiti’s elections, <a href="https://cephaiti.ht/elections-et-droits-de-lhomme-le-cep-prone-le-respect-des-droits-fondamentaux-lors-dun-atelier-consacre-aux-garanties-democratiques/">scheduled for</a> July and October 2027. Civilian casualties or failure to sustain gains could undermine his own government’s credibility.</p>

<h2>Beyond military operations</h2>

<p>The deployment may foreshadow wider regional security arrangements. </p>

<p>El Salvador belongs to the <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/DCPD-202600155">U.S.-backed Shield of the Americas</a>, a coalition launched by Trump in March 2026 to <a href="https://amp.dw.com/en/shield-of-the-americas-trump-launches-regional-coalition/a-76262744">expand military cooperation</a> against drug cartels and other transnational criminal groups.</p>

<p>The Salvadoran operation in Haiti does not formally fall under that initiative, whose <a href="https://www.forth.news/lists/state/CfK5nG2Hm6uuvGtfSJ793">15 signatories</a> have pledged closer security cooperation. But such partnerships could allow regional governments to deploy forces with American logistical support while limiting direct U.S. military involvement. </p>

<p>Although the Salvadoran operation is the latest high-profile example, I have seen similar cycles working in Haiti since the 2000s. U.N. peacekeepers and Haitian police <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20846354/">cleared parts of Cité Soleil between 2007 and 2009</a>, contributing to a decline in kidnappings but failing to deliver lasting security. The <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2016/dec/01/haiti-cholera-outbreak-stain-on-reputation-un-says">U.N. mission later introduced cholera</a> following the 2010 earthquake, killing more than 9,000 people and prompting an eventual apology from the U.N.</p>

<p>Gangs endure because their <a href="https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/article-haitis-elites-should-be-held-accountable-for-backing-gangs/">economic networks survive</a> military offensives. They profit from kidnappings and illicit trade while <a href="https://www.americasquarterly.org/article/flows-of-guns-and-money-are-dooming-haiti/">controlling access</a> to key roads and markets. Removing leaders can <a href="https://my.rusi.org/resource/criminal-governance-politics-of-control-in-latin-america-and-the-caribbean.html">weaken organizations</a> without ending these revenue streams. </p>

<p>While the current Salvadoran offensive may deliver short-term security gains, sustaining them will depend on Haitian institutions maintaining control of recovered territory.</p>

<p>Bukele’s intervention is now an overseas test of a security model with considerable political appeal. But its consequences will ultimately be measured by whether Haitians are safer when foreign forces depart.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296390/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

He also advises governments, private companies, non-profits and international organizations such as the United Nations, the IMF and the World Bank.</span></em></p></content>

<title>You likely have genes that affect how well your medications work – testing for them could improve treatment</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771234/original/file-20261110-78-3z1j9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=68%2C0%2C2053%2C1368&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pharmacogenomics studies how genetics interacts with drugs.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/shaped-colored-pills-royalty-free-image/1258031672">Utku Yilmazturk/iStock via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>All people carry differences in their DNA that could <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040">affect how they respond to medication</a>, according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics.</p>

<p>Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/genomics-and-health/pharmacogenomics/">field of pharmacogenomics</a> studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-prescription-drugs-can-work-differently-for-different-people-168645">liver breaks down a drug</a> and how long it stays in your bloodstream.</p>

<p>But using <a href="https://theconversation.com/can-at-home-dna-tests-predict-how-youll-respond-to-your-medications-pharmacists-explain-the-risks-and-benefits-of-pharmacogenetic-testing-209312">genetic testing to guide prescriptions</a> is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been <a href="https://theconversation.com/uncovering-the-genetic-basis-of-mental-illness-requires-data-and-tools-that-arent-just-based-on-white-people-this-international-team-is-collecting-dna-samples-around-the-globe-185997">done on people of European ancestry</a>, researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else.</p>

<h2>Genetic variants and drugs</h2>

<p>To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=LKG31OkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">and I</a> analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the <a href="https://www.nih.gov/allofus">All of Us Research Program</a>. All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ti50nS7B5vI?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">All of Us seeks to increase the diversity of biomedical research data.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken.</p>

<p>We found that every participant <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040">carried at least one relevant genetic variant</a>, and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications.</p>

<p>Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040">affected by a genetic variant</a> they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions.</p>

<p>These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040">17,704 previously unreported variants</a> in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs. </p>

<p>Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data.</p>

<h2>Improving precision medicine</h2>

<p>Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance <a href="https://theconversation.com/personalized-cancer-treatments-based-on-testing-drugs-quickly-leads-to-faster-treatment-better-outcomes-221469">precision medicine</a>. </p>

<p>However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-prescription-drugs-can-work-differently-for-different-people-168645">affect how the body processes drugs</a>. </p>

<p>Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296352/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
