<title>The ‘religious left’ may be rising – but Black Christian women have been there all along</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771215/original/file-20261110-64-eanaau.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3554%2C2369&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Worshippers during service at Rosemount Missionary Baptist Church in Jackson, Miss., which Democrat Scott Colom visited during his campaign for U.S. Senate.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026Mississippi/cbf7db49ec974babbe05c3f48c1530e9/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=black%20church&amp;currentItemNo=0&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>During campaign season, headlines were full of candidates who spoke openly about their faith – and many of them were Democrats.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.kansascity.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/david-hudnall/article317948881.html">Adam Hamilton</a>, the new senator-elect from Kansas, is pastor of the United States’ largest United Methodist congregation. <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/texas/news/texas-30-congressional-district-election-results-2026/">Frederick Haynes</a>, who will represent a Texas district in the U.S. House of Representatives, is a Baptist pastor. <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/08/16/senate-hopeful-talarico-touts-his-faith-texas-republicans-call-it-blasphemy/">Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico</a> is a Presbyterian seminary student who put a biblical commandment – “Love thy neighbor” – at the center of his campaign.</p>

<p>Since election night, journalists and commentators have attributed a significant amount of credit for the proverbial “Blue Wave” <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6029108/how-religion-helped-democrats-win-control-of-congress?utm_source=substack&amp;utm_medium=email">to the religious left</a>. Although some mention Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton, who is Jewish, <a href="https://religionnews.com/2026/11/04/on-election-night-the-religious-left-is-back/">the focus has been on progressive Christians</a>.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.uncw.edu/profiles/d/delgadod">a scholar of race, gender and religion</a> whose work focuses on <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=-F1k-RAAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">Black Protestant Christianity</a>, I found post-election reporting about a rise in the religious left curious. Voters from many faith traditions did help power the “Blue Wave,” but one often-overlooked group has long been the left’s staunchest supporters: Black Christian women.</p>

<h2>Steady support</h2>

<p>Focus on the “return” of the religious Democrats highlights the contrast between the religious diversity on the left and the <a href="https://www.newsweek.com/white-evangelical-support-for-republicans-ticked-up-despite-blue-tsunami-12672721">allegiance between MAGA Republicans and evangelicals on the right</a>. <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls">According to NBC exit polls</a>, 82% of voters who consider themselves white evangelicals or born-again Christians voted for GOP candidates in 2026. In 2024, 82% of evangelicals in 10 key states <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-elections/exit-polls">voted for President Donald Trump</a>.</p>

<p>But talking about religious Democrats as if they are a new, shiny bauble implies that, until this election, religious progressives have been off the ballot. That is simply not the case, especially when it comes to Black women.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-elections/exit-polls/">Over the last four elections</a>, <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2022-elections/exit-polls/">majorities of both female voters</a> <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-elections/exit-polls">and Black voters</a> <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls">have voted blue</a>. Black women vote for Democrats <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls">by an ever bigger margin</a>: 93%, in 2026 exit polls, compared with 59% of women overall and 86% of Black men. Although Black women account for only 5-7% of Americans, they have been the most consistent Democratic voting bloc.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/12/02/key-facts-about-black-americans-and-religion/">More than 7 in 10 Black Americans are Christian</a>, and the vast majority are Protestant. Another 4% belong to other faiths, including Islam, and 22% are religiously unaffiliated. According to Pew’s 2023-24 <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religious-landscape-study/religious-tradition/historically-black-protestant/">Religious Landscape Survey</a>, 2 in 3 members of Black Protestant denominations are women.</p>

<h2>‘God told me to go’</h2>

<p>Many Black women candidates spoke about faith on the campaign trail.</p>

<p>For example, <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/C8I1ZNix5Fq/?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet">Keisha Lance Bottoms</a>, the governor-elect of Georgia, <a href="https://www.umnews.org/en/news/united-methodists-win-big-in-midterms">attends a</a> <a href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/DfN5wclxzTq/">Methodist church</a>. A few days after her victory, she spoke at the historic <a href="https://www.ebenezeratl.org/our-history/">Ebenezer Baptist Church</a> in Atlanta, pastored by Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia. During her visit, Lance Bottoms recalled that <a href="https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/atlanta/georgia-election-2026-governor-elect-bottoms-speaks-historic-atlanta-church/HK4Z7JD7UBDSHDHK663RIYIKBU/">she had prayed about whether to run for governor</a> and said that “God told me to go.” Her billionaire opponent was a “Goliath,” she said, but “<a href="https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/atlanta/georgia-election-2026-governor-elect-bottoms-speaks-historic-atlanta-church/HK4Z7JD7UBDSHDHK663RIYIKBU/">our God supplied all of our needs</a>.”</p>

<p><a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DZI9WnYlYDd/?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet">Anita Earls</a>, who was re-elected as a judge on the North Carolina Supreme Court, is a longtime member of the <a href="https://www.ame-church.com/our-church/our-history/">African Methodist Episcopal Church</a>.</p>

<p>Among sitting Democrats, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester <a href="https://www.christianpost.com/news/lisa-blunt-rochester-details-why-she-prayed-during-capitol-riot.html">has spoken about her Christian faith</a>. Massachusetts Rep. <a href="https://religionnews.com/2020/11/04/5-faith-facts-the-squad-omar-tlaib-a-pressley-aoc-muslim-catholic-baptist/">Ayanna Pressley</a>, who grew up Baptist, has called herself “<a href="https://pressley.house.gov/2023/10/20/video-pressley-colleagues-faith-leaders-renew-call-for-ceasefire-to-save-lives/">a sister in Christ</a> and a woman of faith. Someone who believes in the power of prayer.”</p>

<p>Each of these women is part of the religious left.</p>

<p>Before them was <a href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/shirley-chisholm">Shirley Chisholm</a>, who became the first Black woman elected to Congress in 1968. Four years later, she was the first Black woman to run for president on the Democratic ticket. Her 1970 memoir, “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/unbought-and-unbossed-shirley-chisholm?variant=40152567545890">Unbought and Unbossed</a>,” recounts her commitment to progressive ideals, ranging from education to women’s reproductive rights, and to her Christian faith.</p>

<p>“America has the laws and the material resources it takes to ensure justice for all its people,” <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/unbought-and-unbossed-shirley-chisholm?variant=40152567545890">she wrote</a>. “What it lacks is the heart, the humanity, the Christian love that it would take. It is perhaps unrealistic to hope that I can help give this nation any of those things, but that is what I believe I have to try to do.”</p>

<h2>Long history</h2>

<p>Before Black women were voted into office, however, they were already <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-women-who-stood-with-martin-luther-king-jr-and-sustained-a-movement-for-social-change-197262">pillars of progressive politics</a>. Historically, Black churches have been more than a place to foster belief. They have also been community-based institutions that fostered social, political and economic justice.</p>

<p>Within Black denominations, men tend to hold senior leadership positions. In his famed book “<a href="https://wwnorton.com/books/9780393870749">The Souls of Black Folk</a>,” sociologist <a href="https://hutchinscenter.fas.harvard.edu/web-dubois">W.E.B. DuBois</a> observed that the Black preacher was also a community “leader, a politician, an orator, a ‘boss,’ an intriguer, an idealist.”</p>

<p>Women’s role was less public, <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/45024509">but no less vital</a>, including social and political organizing. In “<a href="https://www.fortresspress.com/store/product/9780800636036/Witnessing-and-Testifying">Witnessing and Testifying</a>,” religion professor <a href="https://www.spelman.edu/staff/profiles/rosetta-e-ross.html">Rosetta Ross</a> showed how Black women’s faith and activism inspired each other during the Civil Rights Movement. Among the women Ross surveyed is Ella Baker, who organized the initial meeting for what would become the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and often “used Christian scripture to admonish listeners to fight” for freedom.</p>

<p>Women like Baker, <a href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/fannie-lou-hamer">voting rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer</a>, and <a href="https://blackwomensreligiousactivism.org/activists/clara-muhammad/">Clara Muhammad</a>, wife of Nation of Islam founder Elijah Muhammad, show how Black communities’ concerns and faith <a href="https://tupress.temple.edu/books/jesus-jobs-and-justice">often intertwined with progressive politics</a>. In 1958, Nannie Helen Burroughs, <a href="https://nationalhumanitiescenter.org/fellows-books/jesus-jobs-and-justice-african-american-women-and-religion/">founder of the Women’s Auxiliary of the National Baptist Convention</a>, said that African American Christians wanted “<a href="https://tupress.temple.edu/books/jesus-jobs-and-justice">Jesus, jobs and justice</a>.”</p>

<h2>Black, Christian and progressive</h2>

<p>Today, too, faith guides many progressive Black women’s politics and public service. For voting rights activists, for example, casting a ballot <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/IkRHSH_fm6E">is not just a right</a>, <a href="https://www.threads.com/@mspackyetti/post/DfQWAfJGuoB?xmt=AQG0RG5LfTo-19vEzz94McrHxamAYtow3uD9zlIjxYzpxlZ_mc153H6zCkaOgXYzbiTYQjjm&amp;slof=1">but something sacred</a>.</p>

<p>Over the past week, journalists and political pundits have drawn attention to the many different groups that <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6028080/voter-polls-midterms-demographics">moved to the left</a> to fuel Democrats’ midterm victories, including young voters, Latinos, Asian Americans, men and political independents. Black women voters, meanwhile, <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls">have remained steady</a>.</p>

<p>Indeed, history has shown how <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S1743923X23000417">their steadiness</a> helped <a href="https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/takeaway/segments/black-women-role-democratic-party">guide the Democratic Party’s</a> <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/nbcblk/story-black-women-politics-how-we-got-kamala-harris-ascent-n1236528">political and moral compass</a>. And I am willing to wager that they will continue to play an essential role in what the left does between now and 2028.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296110/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Sens.-elect Annie Andrews, James Talarico, and Troy Jackson — all Democrats — walk through the US Capitol as they arrive for new member orientation meetings on November 9, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
We’re a week past the midterms now and the dust has largely settled
Sure, you still have some uncalled House races in a handful of states , and we’re still waiting with bated breath to meet the next senators from Mississippi and Alaska
But even without those final numbers, we can say a couple things for sure: First,  last week’s blue wave was the largest in more than 50 years
And second, Democrats’ real work has only just begun
This week, the incoming members of Congress — roughly seven weeks out from their official debut — are in Washington, DC,  to set up their offices and meet their new coworkers
Democrats still have to choose new leaders or stick with their old ones

And once they’ve reached some sort of consensus on that, they’ll start to confront the final boss: President Donald Trump.  “They’re in control, but they’re really not in control,” Trump told Fox News last week, of the Democrats’ prospects in a split government. “Because they can send over, you know, 50 different great bills that they’re all excited about and I send them back with a nice stamp.” Fortunately, amid all this jockeying and post-election euphoria, we do have some precedent to fall back on
After all, this blue wave was historically big — but not totally unheard-of
Midterm elections also ushered in huge partisan majorities in the early 1970s and 1990s
And that history suggests that Democrats  have won a chance …not a guarantee
Go a little deeper View Link You have to go back to the Watergate era to find a blue wave as big as last week’s

The year was 1974, the vibes were alternatingly grim and groovy, and American voters were looking for change after the scandals of Richard Nixon’s presidency.  Democrats already controlled the House and the Senate, but that year’s midterms ushered in a class of even younger and more liberal lawmakers

And these so-called  Watergate babies came to play: They helped extend a run of post-Watergate reforms that opened up congressional proceedings, required financial disclosures from senior officials, and strengthened oversight of federal agencies
But 52 years later, the 1974 blue wave isn’t exactly remembered as an unrivaled success — for the Dems or for democracy
Ronald Reagan became president just six years later, and both he and other presidents since have weakened the reforms of the mid-’70s

The push to make government more transparent — by inviting television cameras into hearings, for example — also arguably made Congress a more polarized and confrontational place as lawmakers were newly incentivized to be less candid, more performative, and more rigid in their ideology.  Other, more conservative waves have also run up against the limits of congressional power
Strong points to Newt Gingrich’s 1994 “revolution,” which ended four decades of Democratic House control

But that Republican sweep, far from delivering Gingrich’s vision of a dramatically smaller government in one fell swoop, triggered bitter confrontations with President Bill Clinton, including debt-ceiling standoffs and government shutdowns
When major legislation did become law, it required compromise: A sweeping welfare overhaul only passed after Clinton vetoed prior versions twice.  In some ways, these challenges are fairly intuitive
Even when one party controls the White House and both chambers of Congress, it still has to reconcile competing factions and navigate procedural hurdles in the Senate

And when control of those branches is split between parties, as it will be soon, you end up with even bigger obstacles — like a veto-happy president.  Given that, Democratic voters might want to temper their expectations just a little

As my colleague Andrew Prokop laid out earlier this month, Democratic bills will — even in this new, blue environment — likely only pass through compromise or fierce confrontation.  Making electoral history is one thing, as history itself shows
But making legislative history is an altogether tougher proposition

One link for later ➨ Reconsider convenience. “ Friction-maxxing ” is all the rage these days, and while I don’t endorse hassle for its own sake…it’s certainly wise to scrutinize the trade-offs of any new time-saving technology

Gabe Bullard, the author of the new book Against Convenience , suggests the following prompts : What does this tool save me? What does it cost me? And what problem does it solve? Before you go… Did you know… that the word “computer” originally described people ? Before they were machines, computers were workers (often, women) who completed tedious mathematical programs by hand or on analog calculators.  Today’s trivia: The singer Leontyne Price is renowned for her work in which musical genre? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the botanist supervillain in Batman
That would be Poison Ivy, who first debuted 60 years ago in 1966.

title: Why are fewer Black Americans getting GLP-1s?
excerpt: GLP-1s have become the newest celebrity miracle drug, with famous athletes like Serena Williams and Charles Barkley sharing that they’ve used it for weight loss
body: GLP-1s have become the newest celebrity miracle drug, with famous athletes like Serena Williams and Charles Barkley sharing that they’ve used it for weight loss
Drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy have become a status symbol
But before they were famous, GLP-1s were developed to treat Type 2 diabetes, a disease that occurs when a person’s blood sugar becomes too high
It affects nearly 40 million Americans and hits Black Americans especially hard
According to the CDC, about 12 percent of Black adults have diabetes , compared with roughly 7 percent of white adults
Yet when researchers reviewed 26 studies from across the country , they found that Black patients were about 20 percent less likely than white patients to be prescribed newer diabetes drugs
A century ago, doctors called diabetes a “luxury disease” of wealthy white and Jewish people, and many didn’t believe Black people could get the disease at all

Even after the landmark 1985 Heckler Report exposed stark racial disparities in American health, Black patients’ diabetes was often blamed on lifestyle rather than on the housing, food, financial, and healthcare inequities shaping their health
Hosted by Kahlil Greene , this video is part of our series, Kahlil Explains, which unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society
This episode traces the history of race and diabetes in America to unpack why Black patients are still less likely to get access to GLP-1s, and why closing that gap will take more than a prescription

title: A little-known law could upend the dairy industry
excerpt: This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare
body: This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare
Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country
But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system

And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it.  At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies
Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation
Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them

Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef.  But whatever their ultimate market destination, the overwhelming majority of baby cows born in the dairy industry, in California and nationwide, spend their first few months of life housed alone, in individual crates or enclosures

Many of them look like this:  largest calf raiser in California . | Courtesy of Direct Action Everywhere (DxE)" data-portal-copyright="Courtesy of Direct Action Everywhere (DxE)" /> Earlier this year, I wrote at length about that practice

These wooden crates provide each calf about 13 square feet of living space, less than one-tenth the size of a typical parking spot. “We’re talking roughly the size of a coffin,” Vanessa Shakib, a lawyer and co-founder of the Los Angeles-area nonprofit Advancing Law for Animals , told me
Confining calves in this manner is not dissimilar to the use of gestation crates in the pork industry — tiny metal enclosures where pigs barely have room to move
Gestation crates have sparked intense national controversy that’s reached the halls of Congress and the US Supreme Court
But the extreme confinement of dairy calves has not received anywhere close to as much legal and political scrutiny.  In California, there’s an obvious legal problem with calf crates

The state has a plain-English law, Section 597t of its criminal code, that mandates that confined animals be provided an “adequate exercise area.” Though it doesn’t define what constitutes such an area, Shakib and other farm animal advocates argue that it strains credulity to believe the minuscule, barren crates provide one

The practice “is squarely at odds with the plain meaning of the words,” Shakib said.  But California has never enforced that law against calf crates in the state’s powerful dairy industry, where millions of newborn calves have been kept in extreme confinement (nor, apparently, has the law been enforced against any factory farm)

It’s a prime example of agricultural exceptionalism — the doctrine running through American legal and political culture, as Vox’s Kenny Torrella has written , that effectively absolves agribusiness from having to play by the same rules as everyone else.  Shakib and her organization are now hoping to change that.  They’re leading a lawsuit against Hettinga Dairy, a Southern California farm that has kept thousands of calves in individual crates, alleging that it’s violating Section 597t

If the case succeeds, it could create a blueprint for similar challenges statewide, and even spark a broader reckoning within America’s dairy industry.  The case that could transform how dairy calves are treated Advancing Law for Animals just filed suit on behalf of the Caru Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, a California animal protection nonprofit seeking a court ruling that the calf crates violate state law
The case names Hettinga Dairy and related defendants in connection with a  San Jacinto, California, facility that specializes in raising calves

The most recent available records from California’s State Water Resources Control Board report the farm’s animal population as 4,200 calves.  Such facilities, often known as “calf ranches” or “calf nurseries,” have become increasingly central to the US dairy business — as we wrote earlier this year, they “raise calves on dairy farms’ behalf during the fragile infant stage in which they’re too young to bring in any revenue.”  Caru SPCA (which is formerly known as the Animal Legal Defense Fund Cruelty Prevention Unit) flew drone cameras over the Hettinga facility earlier this year to document the calf housing there, filming the small wooden crates that are common in California and the Southwest, typically providing less than 15 square feet of space per calf

Many dairy farms and calf ranches use a different, plastic hutch design that provides more space, but the smaller wooden hutches remain widespread.  Calves typically spend about two months in these hutches before being moved into larger group pens; the lawsuit alleges that Hettinga keeps them in crates for around nine weeks.  “Calves are trapped for months, even in summer heat, unable to stretch their limbs or move freely,” the lawsuit alleges

Under 597t, “animals have a statutory right to minimal movement, and Defendants systematically violate that right daily, creating immense and ongoing suffering.” That San Jacinto farm is part of a broader network of dairy farms and calf-raising facilities linked to the Hettingas, a prominent dairy family whose farms collectively confine thousands of calves and cows across California, according to state public records
Most consumers have never heard of Hettinga, nor of the hundreds of other industrial dairies and calf-raising farms across California that operate largely out of public view
But the Hettingas also have a presence on grocery store shelves: According to the brand’s website, the family also owns Sarah Farms , a mass-market milk label in the Southwestern US
Vox emailed a list of questions about the allegations in the lawsuit to multiple contacts associated with Hettinga businesses
An employee at GH Processing , a Hettinga family-associated dairy plant in Arizona, confirmed receiving the email and said she would pass it on to colleagues in California

No one responded to Vox’s questions by publication time.  A representative from the California water board told Vox that the 2024 annual report for the San Jacinto calf facility identified Hein and Ellen Hettinga as the farm’s operators
But state regulators have not received the 2025 report, which was due in January 2026, and could not verify the facility’s current ownership

Hein Hettinga, who built the family’s dairy empire, died in 2023; Ellen, his wife, is one of the defendants named in the lawsuit.  Dairy industry trade groups often defend calf crates, arguing that they allow farmers to provide each animal with individualized care and reduce their exposure to pathogens

Whether that’s true is contested — some industry veterinarians endorse that view, while others maintain that it’s based on a narrow view of calves’ well-being and that properly managed social housing need not harm their physical health

Even within the industry, there’s growing acknowledgement that isolation is harmful to calves, and that it would be better for dairy farms to transition to a different system.  A 2023 assessment of calf welfare from the European Food Safety Authority — the EU agency that provides scientific guidance on animal welfare — found “no locomotor play behavior possible” for calves given a space allowance of about 16 square feet each
A calf in such confinement “is expected to spend most of its time lying down because no other activities can be performed,” the review states

To fully express natural behaviors like galloping, jumping, and kicking, it recommends that calves housed alone be allotted 318 square feet each, and calves housed in groups be allotted 215 square feet each, though it notes that even smaller increases in space could meaningfully improve their welfare.  Guidelines from Calf Care and Quality Assurance, a US industry-created animal care program, state that “individually housed calves have a harder time coping with changes in housing and diet and may have cognitive and developmental disadvantages, including poor learning skills and deficient social skills.” Temple Grandin, the famed livestock scientist at Colorado State University, has written that “calves should be raised with other calves, not in isolation.” They are, after all, intensely social herd animals.  Regardless of the industry’s opinion on the practice, though, 597t makes no exception for livestock industry standard practices, the way some states’ animal cruelty laws do. “It doesn’t matter whether this defendant or whether the dairy industry believes solitary confinement of baby animals serves a useful purpose,” Shakib said. “California law here is crystal clear — it requires an adequate exercise area

Industry custom or convenience does not erase that requirement.” California’s animal cruelty double standard The ubiquitous confinement of dairy calves in tiny crates remains poorly understood by the general public, and even, to some extent, within the animal protection movement
That is because, for many years, animal advocates focused their campaigning against extreme confinement in the dairy industry on veal, the notorious specialty meat made from male dairy calves

Those efforts helped bring about California’s Proposition 12, a landmark law passed in 2018 that bans certain forms of extreme confinement, including tiny crates that used to be the norm in veal production
Any veal raised or sold in California must now come from calves allotted at least 43 square feet of living space each

But the overwhelming share of California’s dairy calves are not raised for veal and thus get no protection under Prop 12, even as many members of the public may assume the problem of extreme confinement of calves has been solved.  In the last few years, however, a small wave of animal advocates have been drawing attention to the continued plight of dairy calves

The animal rights group Direct Action Everywhere (DxE) over the last year has documented and mapped calf confinement across California, including at Grimmius Cattle Company, the largest calf raiser in the state and the subject of Vox’s earlier reporting

This fall, DxE investigator Lewis Bernier obtained footage showing calves from a dairy farm that the group said supplies to Land O’Lakes being transported to Grimmius, where the newborn animals are raised in the same standard, approximately 13-square-foot wooden hutches

Land O’Lakes did not respond to requests for comment.  The crates aren’t the only problem Beyond extreme confinement in crates,  DxE’s investigations have surfaced allegations of overt abuse of calves — including animals being kicked, punched, and pulled by their ears and tails — at calf ranches and dairy farms throughout California

Drone footage taken earlier this year at a dairy farm that DxE linked to Leprino Foods — a major cheese supplier that reportedly sells to Domino’s, Papa John’s, and Pizza Hut, among others — shows calves being kicked, pushed, pulled by their ears, and thrown to the ground

title: How Cornell has deepened college women’s nihilism about campus assault
excerpt: Josephine Campos, 19, was feeling optimistic when she started her sophomore year at the University of Vermont
body: Josephine Campos, 19, was feeling optimistic when she started her sophomore year at the University of Vermont
After spending the last few years focusing on herself, she was ready to date
She was going to be intentional, explore her options on the apps and at parties, put herself out there

But in September, when news broke of a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit against several men alleging they coerced her into taking drugs and then raped her, Campos told me she reconsidered. “Wait, do I really want to be doing this right now?” she asked herself.   For many college women, it’s a fair question
In the time since Campos first learned of the lawsuit, the public has reacted with outrage over the school’s handling of the incident
The New York attorney general appointed a former federal prosecutor to investigate the allegations — yet, none of the seven accused men, who deny wrongdoing, have been criminally charged

The university’s faculty senate voted no confidence in Cornell’s administration “to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault.” Cornell’s board of trustees, however, said it still has faith in the administration .  And just this week, New York Focus uncovered a 2023 lawsuit against Cornell in which two students alleged the school did not take their accusations of sexual assault seriously

This mirrors what many women on America’s college campuses are feeling right now: Despite decades of advocacy and education around sexual violence, these incidents are still not taken seriously.  Campos was just 10 years old when the Me Too movement exposed the prevalence of sexual assault in America
Today’s college students had reason to believe that the harrowing stories and bravery from young women like Chanel Miller , Emma Sulkowicz , and the survivors of Larry Nassar could change the culture
Now, more than a decade later, the Cornell allegations represent another tipping point — where women’s safety would finally be taken seriously

But the young women who spoke with me for this story don’t see that happening any time soon.  Why I reported this When news broke of Jane Doe’s lawsuit against Cornell and the seven members of a fraternity she alleges raped her, I was both horrified by the details and optimistic that the public outcry would amount to systemic change

I wanted to speak to young women about their dating lives, their conversations with friends and boyfriends, and student attitudes to learn if anything was different on college campuses since I was in school
Many say they still feel overwhelming pressure to protect themselves because they believe the institutions charged with their care have failed them

After waves of outcry following each high-profile campus assault case, young women are losing hope that meaningful progress will ever materialize.  “I would like to think it would be a turning point, but I’m just not sure,” 22-year-old Hannah Butler, a senior at Western Carolina University, told me. “I’m not sure because I feel like we hear so many stories of campus sexual assaults and nothing ever really happens a lot of the time
It’s just so unfortunately normalized

I’m worried that this is going to be another, ‘Oh crap, that happens,’ and then everybody continues on because everyone’s so desensitized to it now.” “Cover your drinks”  Campus sexual assault is common

A 2017 study concluded that the “one in five” statistic that is often used to quantify it is “is a reasonably accurate average across women and campuses.” In New York, a state that requires schools to report sexual assault, more than 25,000 incidents of sexual misconduct involving a student were documented between 2018 and 2024

Today, women continue to bear the brunt of speaking out mistreatment and sexual assault: They lean on “ Are we sharing boyfriends? ” Facebook groups and other whisper networks to voice their negative experiences with certain men and to warn other women

Most acts of sexual violence are not reported to authorities, and even fewer actually make national news.  But when cases do capture the public’s attention — as Cornell’s did — they bring awareness to the prevalence of the problem

Campos said the Cornell case opened her eyes to the widespread issue of campus rape, and said the ongoing news coverage has made it easier for her and her friends to discuss their past sexual experiences, stories that might not have otherwise come to light. “It’s not just happening at these really big schools,” Campos said. “You forget that it happens everywhere until you hear someone talking about it and then you’re like, ‘Oh wait, that happens here.’” Butler said she and her friends have had similar conversations informed by their own experiences with sexual harassment and abuse
Butler remembered one of her friends texting their group chat for help while being cornered in the laundry room by a man

Others have been sexually assaulted but didn’t even realize it at the time that what happened to them had a name.  “What our conversations generally sound like is shocked and horrified,” Butler told me, “but not super surprised.” Gen Z has grown up in a precarious world full of perceived risks and threats , who have practiced school shooter drills since kindergarten; they are a generation that highly values safety
This attentiveness has filtered into their dating lives, too

Josie Stoffan, a 21-year-old senior at the University of Michigan, told me that being hyper aware is already part of their mindset. “I feel like it hasn’t really changed because we’ve already been, I don’t know, very vigilant about everything going on,” she said

This awareness stems, in part, from discussions on social media where young women share tips on how to avoid potentially dangerous situations, Stoffan said.  This heightened vigilance is true for Campos, too
Despite her initial hesitations, she has decided to date after all — but she makes sure her friends have access to her location, and she only meets during the day in public locations
Butler’s friend group took location-sharing a step further: They’ve purchased trackers to monitor each other’s whereabouts
They also avoid alcohol on first dates — water only. “Girls are always taught to cover your drinks and be safe,” Butler said
This undercurrent of fear and vigilance has swelled beyond the student body in recent weeks
At Pennsylvania State University’s Beaver campus, nurse Jessica Judy has fielded fresh questions from students who pass through her office that she believes was spurred by the Cornell outcry

Others have shared their outrage with her, their support of Jane Doe, their apprehension with dating. “Students are a little bit more leery now after hearing what potentially could happen,” Judy told Vox. “I think that they are really thinking things through and there is a small bit of fear there.” Following many highly publicized incidents of sexual violence, news reports and social media commentary can empower people to speak out against rape or share their own experience , which was especially true in the years following Me Too

Society has made progress in recognizing the severity of these crimes and supporting victims, Elizabeth Armstrong , a sociologist at the University of Michigan who studies campus sexual assault, told my colleague Rachel Cohen Booth
But, Armstrong noted, most college campuses lack adequate resources for survivors of campus rape: mental health support, learning accommodations, and perhaps refunded tuition

Judy believes her students, both men and women, would benefit from more comprehensive sexual education about what consent is and how it can change within a single encounter. “Is it voluntary? Is it enthusiastic? Has something changed?” she said. “I think that there’s an intimidation for some students, I’ve noticed, to really ask questions or set boundaries.” But this responsibility to self-educate, to communicate, and to suss out whether a date is safe still falls on women

Shortly after learning about the Cornell case from social media — especially the details of the fraternity members’ group chat — Zoie King, a 21-year-old senior at San José State University, began asking her boyfriend what he and his friends discuss in theirs. “I definitely think it’s more, for me, asking questions like, ‘Oh, your friend hooked up with that girl
What did he say?’” King said. “You learn a little bit more about the friends and you’re like, ‘I don’t really love that
Oh, that’s kind of weird.’” King was also taken aback by how differently she and her boyfriend’s attitudes toward safety

While she hardly ever walks alone at night, her boyfriend doesn’t bat an eye. “For him, it was just very surprising hearing how different women, especially women in college, see the world, how vigilant they have to be all the time,” King said. “It’s a bunch of frat men around you, and they don’t really care” It’s impossible to separate the Cornell allegations from the longstanding issues with Greek life: Hazing , rampant alcohol and drug use, and an intense party culture can create unsafe scenarios for both women and men
One study found that fraternity membership was correlated with sexual aggression
Fraternity houses are among the most common locations on college campuses where students reported being sexually assaulted

title: Could this bacteria save coral reefs from the heat?
excerpt: Coral reefs off the coast of Abu Dhabi. | John Burt/Courtesy of Amin Mohamed As extreme heat destroys more coral reefs, scientists are racing to find new — and
body: Coral reefs off the coast of Abu Dhabi. | John Burt/Courtesy of Amin Mohamed As extreme heat destroys more coral reefs, scientists are racing to find new — and sometimes unexpected — ways to keep them alive
Some are trying to encourage corals to reproduce more , while others are testing for heat fitness using picnic coolers
A recent study has a new approach, and it comes from an unexpected place: the corals’ own microbiome
Corals, like humans, have a multitude of bacteria living in and on them

It has long been assumed that this diverse population of microbes serves a role similar to the bacteria in our own bodies — helping the host while getting a home and a steady source of nutrition in return

But many of the specific functions of corals’ microbiomes remained unclear, and every coral colony, even among corals of the same species that are right next to each other, can have different microbiomes.  This new study, published in Nature Microbiology , shows that one bacteria type called Endozoicomonas , which is found in a wide variety of coral species all over the world, can produce hormones that help the coral they studied deal with heat stress
It could potentially make other species of coral more resistant to the effects of extreme heat and prevent them from bleaching as well
That would be a big deal for the coral themselves, which are incredibly unique organisms with a wide variety of species across the planet

It would also help the thousands of aquatic creatures that call coral reefs home, from endangered sea turtles and reef sharks to the clownfish that inspired Finding Nemo.  The Persian Gulf has some of the hottest, saltiest seas on the planet, which makes it a particularly harsh environment for the coral living there
August, when temperatures are at their peak, is particularly rough, explained Amin Mohamed , a researcher at NYU Abu Dhabi and lead author of the study

Extreme heat breaks down the relationship between the coral animals and their symbiotic algae, starving the coral and turning them a ghostly white in events known as “bleaching.” As climate change makes extreme heat more common, more and more reefs around the world are bleaching, putting them at risk of dying altogether
But heat itself doesn’t always tell the full story

Even though water temperatures in the Persian Gulf during the summer of 2016, when Mohamed and his colleagues collected their first coral samples, reached as high as 34 degrees Celsius (93.2 degrees Fahrenheit), not all of the coral they studied — an endangered stony coral Acropora pharaonis — reacted to the heat in the same way.  “We found that some colonies [of this species] developed a heat-related disease called white band syndrome; but we found other colonies that remained healthy — with no sign of disease whatsoever — at the same temperature,” Mohamed told me. “So this got us very interested in understanding what is behind the mechanisms keeping these [corals] healthy and stable.”  When they went searching for an answer to explain the difference, they found that the coral colonies with the disease had lost the Endozoicomonas bacteria living in their microbiome, while the ones that were still healthy also had a healthy population of resident Endozoicomonas

And when they looked even more closely, they found that the bacteria were doing something that bacteria usually don’t do: They were producing the hormones testosterone and progesterone, which exist in many multicellular organisms (including us humans) but are rarely found in bacteria.  Corals themselves usually only produce testosterone and progesterone during spawning events, which happen once a year

And during marine heat waves, Mohamed said, “the coral aren’t thinking about sex at all.”  But the hormones produced by the bacteria aren’t used for reproduction: Instead, the researchers found out, they help regulate the coral’s immune system
The progesterone is the most important of the two during these events

It seems to keep the coral’s immune system from spinning out of control and using up an excessive amount of the coral’s energy, which could leave it too depleted to recover after the heat passes.  “It’s a really exciting and interesting study,” said Rebecca Vega Thurber, a coral microbiologist and Director of the Marine Science Institute at the University of California Santa Barbara, who was unaffiliated with the study — but read it with her lab for a weekly study-reading club. “There’s been a lot of hypotheses about what the bacterial components of the coral are actually doing, and actually demonstrating it is a really important step forward,” she said. “I also really like this study’s connection to temperature stress, which is the most important stressor for coral reefs right now.” The study comes on the heels of another report , from September, that showed treating coral reefs with probiotic bacteria ahead of a heat wave in the Red Sea helped prevent bleaching

While that study didn’t use Endozoicomonas as one of the bacteria in the probiotics, Mohamed said it might make sense to study whether including it in future probiotic treatments could further improve their effectiveness.  Thurber also said researchers could think about focusing on the testosterone and progesterone themselves — after all, she pointed out, it’s far easier and cheaper to synthesize the hormones than create giant probiotic cultures — and use them to treat coral ahead of heat events

But, she pointed out, suppressing the immune response during heat waves also opens corals up to the possibility of being more easily infected by opportunistic bacteria that would hurt them rather than help them

And if coral restorers went down that route, they might find themselves in a cycle of treating coral with the hormones ahead of a heat event and then giving them antibiotics to fend off invading harmful bacteria.  “Just because you think you have this great bioengineered thing doesn’t mean it’ll work,” Thurber said. “Once you add it, you have no idea what’s gonna happen in the real world.” It’s unclear, for example, what would happen to other animals in the area if restorers decided to try treating the coral with hormones or whether bacterial strains would evolve (to become less helpful or potentially harmful) after they were applied. “Still, the paper gives us ideas about mechanisms that we can use to prevent or mitigate coral decline,” she said. “This is cool science that gives us good ideas about how to move forward.”  As things stand, the factors driving the heat waves and coral bleaching — namely fossil fuel emissions driving global climate change — aren’t going away yet
Until they do, it seems worth exploring new ways, even if they’re a little unorthodox, to help the coral survive.

title: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI —Grace Huckins As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI
Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy
I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor

But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.  “We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI

title: Evolving metal extraction processes
excerpt: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting
body: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible
Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago
Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence

According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience
That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments

Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions
Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control
EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways
The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production
Laboratory work revealed broader potential
Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions
They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed
The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness

Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology Source : Outokumpu Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world

Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT. “The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore
Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches

The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste

Innovation happens at the boundaries EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies
Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering

With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work. “Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn
Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production
Building a technology platform A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform
Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications
Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources
The initial application becomes only the starting point. “The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing
The future of materials companies The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy
Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives
The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027
The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030
Beyond producing low-CO 2 , chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum

The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today? The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on
Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore
It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

title: GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect
url:
<title>GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771211/original/file-20261110-64-wbwdre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5358%2C3572&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Millions of people worldwide take GLP-1 medications.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/still-life-of-the-new-wegovy-semaglutide-tablets-with-out-news-photo/2258364671">Michael Siluk/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a <a href="https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential">potential link to a rare eye condition</a> that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026. The eye condition is called <a href="https://www.aao.org/eyenet/article/naion-diagnosis-and-management">non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy</a>, or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/5601-stroke">stroke</a> of the eye.</p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://ziyadalaly.com/">clinician and epidemiologist</a> who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.9917">link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION</a>.</p>

<p>Millions of people around the world take these medications – including <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/712157/glp-usage-reaches-new-high.aspx">30 million in the U.S.</a> – to <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK551568/">treat diabetes and obesity</a> and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are also being investigated for an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-024-03412-w">expanding list of clinical conditions</a>. </p>

<p>The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so.</p>

<p>Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect.</p>

<h2>What is NAION?</h2>

<p>NAION is an injury to the <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/22261-optic-nerve">optic nerve</a>, which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow. Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness. </p>

<p>These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment. Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/fQVq8mtsVog?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">NAION, an injury to the optic nerve, can cause sudden loss of vision.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>



<h2>How did the FDA identify the connection?</h2>

<p>As use of GLP-1 drugs increased – particularly since <a href="https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/952441">2021, when they were approved for obesity</a> – cases of NAION began to emerge. A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link. It reported <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2024.2296">an increased risk of the eye condition</a> among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug. </p>

<p>To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the <a href="https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential">FDA first compiled data</a> from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs. Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients – 78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison. </p>

<p>Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug. This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs.</p>

<p>In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of <a href="https://www.fda.gov/safety/fdas-sentinel-initiative">sentinel programs</a> that track the real-world safety of approved medications. They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024.</p>

<p>Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1. Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000. This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs.</p>

<h2>Is there other evidence of the risk?</h2>

<p>Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent <a href="https://doi.org/10.2337/dc25-1238">association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION</a>. </p>

<p>For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.9917">600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes</a> starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years. For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication. In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients. </p>

<p>That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients. For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A schematic drawing of the anatomy of the human eye, including the optic nerve" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=528&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=528&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=528&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is an injury to the optic nerve caused by a disruption in blood flow.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/human-eye-anatomy-diagram-in-flat-design-on-royalty-free-illustration/2156319135">Blueastro/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes. It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this.</p>

<p>The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide. It concluded that this eye condition is a <a href="https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/news/prac-concludes-eye-condition-naion-very-rare-side-effect-semaglutide-medicines-ozempic-rybelsus-wegovy">very rare side effect of semaglutide</a> and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect.</p>

<h2>The upshot for patients</h2>

<p>The risk of NAION with GLP-1 drugs is likely real. All the evidence – the FDA’s two analyses, the real-world studies conducted by independent researchers and the fact that two regulators reached the same view independently – points in the same direction. </p>

<p>But in terms of the total number of people who are likely to experience this side effect, the risk is small. In my view, this makes the FDA’s warning not a cause for alarm but rather an unlikely but not impossible outcome that both clinicians and patients should be aware of. </p>

<p>Clinicians should discuss it with their patients before prescribing a GLP-1 drug – and patients should be educated on the symptoms of NAION and how to tell if they are experiencing it.</p>

<p>Patients should also seek immediate care at the earliest signs of vision problems.  For patients who have previously had NAION or who already have <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2021.618353">risk factors for it</a>, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia and kidney disease, careful discussion weighing the risks and benefits is important.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296237/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Pa. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s popularity and ‘get sh-t done’ attitude might not cut it in crowded 2028 Democratic field – but he has options</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770381/original/file-20261105-64-kp8pjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro arrives onstage to declare victory in his reelection bid on Nov. 3, 2026.

</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/democratic-gov-josh-shapiro-arrives-onstage-to-declare-news-photo/2302978410">Joe Lamberti via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/2026-midterm-elections-178375">2026 midterm elections</a> swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “<a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/massive-blue-wave-just-hit-053500218.html">massive</a>.”</p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/pennsylvania-governor-results/">winning more than 60% of the vote</a> – something that has been accomplished only <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_elections">twice before in the modern era</a> in the Keystone State.</p>

<p>Not only did Shapiro wipe the floor with his opponent Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, but he also helped flip four U.S. House seats from red to blue. His coattails <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/09/campaign-finance-pennsylvania-governor-josh-shapiro-stacy-garrity-downballot-elections/">benefited down-ballot candidates</a>, helping Democrats solidify their control of the state House and <a href="https://theconversation.com/pennsylvania-democrats-now-have-power-to-push-forward-on-election-reform-marijuana-legalization-and-minimum-wage-increases-295731">flip the state Senate as well</a>.</p>

<p>Shapiro’s political stock in Pennsylvania is riding high.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://www.ship.edu/academics/cas/department-of-political-and-social-inquiry/faculty-and-staff-poli-sci/allison-dagnes-bio/">political science professor</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&amp;as_sdt=0%2C39&amp;q=alison+dagnes&amp;btnG=">political media researcher</a> in central Pennsylvania, and many of my former students work in Harrisburg. Some are Democrats working for or around the governor; others are Republicans working in different corners of state government. All are finely tuned to the political gossip that swirls around a successful politician whose star is on the rise. It is the worst-kept secret in American politics that Josh Shapiro wants to be president.</p>

<p>I’ve met the governor a handful of times and can attest to his George Clooney-level charisma. He’s a hard worker, has maintained a remarkably clean political profile, and is from many accounts a genuinely nice dude.</p>

<p>And yet, there are plenty of reasons his ambitions may require some careful timing, regardless of his personal strengths.</p>

<h2>A reputation for getting stuff done</h2>

<p>Shapiro’s political victories didn’t just happen. Over the past four years, he has worked <a href="https://theconversation.com/gov-josh-shapiro-has-a-reputation-for-getting-things-done-in-pennsylvania-but-not-necessarily-things-all-democrats-like-235854">to demonstrate bipartisan competence</a> as Pennsylvania’s chief executive, adopting an expression he uses frequently: “<a href="https://apnews.com/article/josh-shapiro-pennsylvania-swear-word-slogan-45db6d5d09a3a1e39bd13f4af70d1e23">get sh-t done</a>.”</p>

<p>Now, with Democrats holding the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly, <a href="https://www.politico.com/newsletters/playbook/2026/11/04/after-the-flood-01148513">Shapiro told reporters</a>: “We got the power now, the House, the Senate. We have to deliver.” </p>

<p>Shapiro’s <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/30/josh-shapiro-pennsylvania-gubernatorial-race-2028-01137443">approval ratings have remained strong</a>, consistent with his reelection margins. That’s unusual in a state that has swung back and forth between supporting <a href="https://www.electionreturns.pa.gov/_ENR/General/SummaryResults?ElectionID=54&amp;ElectionType=G&amp;IsActive=0">Donald Trump in 2016</a>, <a href="https://www.electionreturns.pa.gov/_ENR/General/SummaryResults?ElectionID=83&amp;ElectionType=G&amp;IsActive=0">Joe Biden in 2020</a> and <a href="https://www.electionreturns.pa.gov/General/SummaryResults?ElectionID=105&amp;ElectionType=G&amp;IsActive=0">Trump again in 2024</a>, each time by fewer than 2 percentage points.</p>

<p>If Shapiro is indeed <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5822245-josh-shapiro-2028-speculation-national-action-network/">seriously eyeing the White House</a>, his current popularity will certainly serve him well. But winning the presidency is an enormous undertaking, particularly in a crowded field.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Man in black T-shirt and black framed glasses holds a pint of Guinness and waves yellow rally towel in a bar" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gov. Josh Shapiro tends bar and meets with constituents at a Pittsburgh Steelers watch party at the Cork Harbour Pub in Pittsburgh on Oct. 25, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/pennsylvania-democratic-gubernatorial-candidate-gov-josh-news-photo/2301535648">Jeff Swensen via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Stiff competition in 2028</h2>

<p>With Trump unable to run in 2028, the next presidential election will feature open seats for both parties and likely attract many candidates. Democrats, in particular, have a <a href="https://punchbowl.news/article/campaigns/dems-2028-campaign/">deep bench of attractive potential contenders</a>.</p>

<p>There are so many possibilities that Shapiro could find himself running against people very much like him: younger centrists, swing-state politicians and accomplished elected officials with solid records. Consider just a few names that could be part of the conversation: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel. </p>

<p>Shapiro would have to find a way to distinguish himself in a field filled with candidates who can make many of the same arguments about their experience, political appeal and accomplishments. That’s a tall order. A Plan B might be wise.</p>

<h2>Options beyond the White House</h2>

<p>Fortunately for Shapiro, other choices abound.</p>

<p>He could run for the Senate in 2028 against incumbent John Fetterman, <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/6208182-ahmed-moor-challenges-fetterman/">if Fetterman seeks reelection</a>. This would be a twofer: Shapiro would continue his rise in politics, and he would likely beat a guy he apparently does not like. The two <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/12/us/politics/john-fetterman-josh-shapiro-pennsylvania.html">reportedly don’t speak</a>, much less get along.</p>

<p>Shapiro could also position himself for a vice presidential nomination by attaching himself to another 2028 hopeful. This would buy him time to build his national profile, allow the presidential field to sort itself out and potentially put him in a strong position for another run at the White House down the road. It would also give him an opportunity to demonstrate that he can work effectively on a national stage.</p>

<p>Or he could angle for a Cabinet post. The federal government has undergone <a href="https://www.city-journal.org/article/doge-spending-cuts-civil-service-elon-musk">significant restructuring under DOGE</a> and Trump’s executive orders. Should a Democrat win the White House in 2028, rebuilding federal agencies and restoring institutional capacity will be a monumental undertaking. Shapiro could be an attractive candidate for a major administrative role.</p>

<p>The bottom line for Shapiro is that he will need to distinguish himself from a crowded field of Democrats by emphasizing his statewide victories in a major swing state, impressive fundraising ability and a political voice that <a href="https://www.tiktok.com/@msnow/video/7421241756592737579?_r=1&amp;refer=player_v1&amp;referer_video_id=7421241756592737579&amp;referrer">can evoke Barack Obama</a> without alienating either his party or the broader electorate. That’s a tricky feat, even for the most talented politicians.</p>

<p>But Nov. 3, 2026, showed us that he knows how to make sh-t happen. Whatever he decides, the next two years will be important for Shapiro, consequential for Democrats, and fascinating for political scientists like me, who will be watching events unfold with a keen eye and, probably, a bucket of popcorn.</p>

<p><em>Read more of our stories about <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/philadelphia-pennsylvania-news">Philadelphia and Pennsylvania</a>, or sign up for our Philadelphia <a href="https://tcphilly.substack.com/">newsletter on Substack</a>.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295841/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
