<title>Students creating documentaries with scientists deepens STEM belonging and public trust in science</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769824/original/file-20261103-64-o22b4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4000%2C2666&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Communications and media studies student Evan Leong documents scientists breeding disease-resistant crops. </span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Ava Medberry</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Marine scientists navigate autonomous <a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/atlantic-crossing/">glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean</a> and along the <a href="https://beyondtheice.rutgers.edu/">West Antarctic Peninsula</a>, collecting data to help predict storm intensity.</p>

<p>When farmers’ fields are destroyed by an unknown pathogen, <a href="https://fieldsofdevotion.rutgers.edu/">plant scientists spend years</a> breeding new varieties of disease-resistant food crops. </p>

<p>A team of microbiologists <a href="https://mysteriesof9north.marine.rutgers.edu/">explore deep-sea volcanoes</a> in search of organisms that may contain anticancer compounds. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe src="https://player.vimeo.com/video/1239976215" width="500" height="281" frameborder="0" webkitallowfullscreen="" mozallowfullscreen="" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The science-in-action model teaches students to create documentaries that show the scientific research process.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>These are passionate people who are dedicated to seeking solutions to real-world problems. They are also the main characters in science documentaries produced in the <a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/">Rutgers Immersive Learning Science Storytelling Lab</a> that I oversee. Our lab pairs students with working scientists to co-create documentaries about research as it happens, while earning experiential learning credit.</p>

<p>At a time when <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/11/14/americans-trust-in-scientists-positive-views-of-science-continue-to-decline/">confidence in science is declining</a>, I was approached by scientists who wanted their authentic research stories communicated to broad audiences.</p>

<p>I am an educator, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XRI_2kgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">a researcher and anthropologist</a>, and <a href="https://denaseidel.com/">a science filmmaker</a> who has been making science documentaries with Rutgers students and researchers since 2008. The science-in-action storytelling model I developed is intended to make the human journey of science visible to the public. Our stories communicate the process, motivations and integrity behind science, which <a href="https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10805-026-09732-5">helps earn public confidence and trust in science</a>.</p>

<p>I also partner with STEM learning researchers to gauge whether our documentaries increase the relatability of scientists, increase public understanding of scientific processes and help students find belonging in STEM.</p>

<h2>Our storytelling process</h2>

<p><a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/creation-process/">Science-in-action storytelling</a> is composed of five steps that support student-scientist relationships. </p>

<p>First, the storytellers develop trust with the participating university scientists. This trust stems from shared respect and a mutual understanding of the co-creation process. </p>

<p>The scientists then invite storytellers into their labs and field sites, where we capture their research processes in real time. This is Step 2.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Student recording a woman in a red dress on a beach boardwalk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Undergraduate philosophy major Ben Lerner was invited to accompany oceanographers to Barbados to make the documentary ‘Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet.’</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Leah Hopson</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our professional storytelling team, which includes students, then documents scientists conducting research, including experiments and data collection, as they describe the why and how of their work. Depending on the complexity of the project, we collect dozens to hundreds of hours of science-in-action video footage. </p>

<p>Importantly, this video data is maintained in our storytelling lab, as it often includes recordings of federally funded research. Maintaining the video data repository is a key component to establishing and sustaining trust with the participating scientists.</p>

<p>Step 3 invites students to immerse themselves in the video data and begin shaping the footage into documentary scenes, constructed using only the scientists’ words, without narration. As they analyze hours of footage, our students learn about the authentic scientific processes; in doing so, they participate in research through the process of storytelling. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Young woman at a laptop editing film footage." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Master’s student Shaniya Utamidata directs a 26-minute documentary called ‘Where the Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore,’ about scientists studying estuary biodiversity.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Dena K. Seidel</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our students are not graded on their documentary skills, nor are they required to make a film. Instead, they are graded on the science they learn through the storytelling process.</p>

<p>Step 4 requires that the students share drafts of their documentary scenes with the featured scientist to verify the accuracy of the science communicated. This step is part of the foundational trust agreement with the scientists but is also an opportunity for the students to personally connect with scientists.</p>

<p>For Step 5, our lab works to distribute the documentaries to a wide variety of audiences, including the general public. Here we partner with STEM learning experts to assess audiences’ understanding of and trust in the science communicated in the film and audience perceptions of the featured scientists.</p>

<h2>Reach far beyond the lab</h2>

<p>Our completed science-in-action documentaries have reached audiences far beyond the university. Our National Science Foundation-funded “<a href="https://beyondtheice.rutgers.edu/">Antarctic Edge: 70° South</a>” had a theatrical release and aired on Netflix. “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/atlantic-crossing/">Atlantic Crossing</a>” was broadcast on PBS stations and was included in a <a href="https://journals.ku.edu/jcel/article/view/22838/21753">three-year Smithsonian exhibit</a>. “<a href="https://fieldsofdevotion.rutgers.edu/watch/">Fields of Devotion</a>” was shared by the Association of American Universities as part of its <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NoYWvD6tAHw">campaign to increase public trust in science</a>. And our lab’s newest long-form documentary, “<a href="https://mysteriesof9north.marine.rutgers.edu/">Mysteries of 9° North</a>,” co-created with 14 undergraduates and featuring scientists studying life at deep-sea volcanoes, will be released to the public in early 2027.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Dozens of people sitting in the audience as students introduce a film screening." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=335&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=335&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=335&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Students introduce the first work-in-progress screening of the National Science Foundation-supported, feature-length documentary ‘Mysteries of 9° North’ at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Sean Feuer</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our surveys capture how these science documentaries change audience understanding of science and how it is done. For example, after screening “<a href="https://beyondtheice.rutgers.edu/">Antarctic Edge</a>,” viewers’ self-reported <a href="https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2022.1049648/full">understanding of climate change rose from 71% to 91%</a>. On a 15-item knowledge quiz, average scores rose, with gains of up to 24 percentage points on the concepts they knew least about.</p>

<h2>Creating belonging for students in STEM</h2>

<p>When 102 undergraduates were asked what made the scientists in “<a href="https://fieldsofdevotion.rutgers.edu/watch/">Fields of Devotion</a>” relatable, they named passion for the subject (72%), desire to help others (71%) and commitment to their work (70%).</p>

<p>Our survey results also suggest that students who participated in the lab gained confidence and feelings of belonging in a science community. Undergraduates who once said they did not feel “smart enough” reported that <a href="https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2022.1049648/full">they could now see themselves as scientists</a>. All participating students reported that their collaboration with scientists positively transformed their understanding of science. </p>

<p>Nonscience majors gained a deep understanding of the scientific process, while science majors gained rare access to research outside their own disciplines. </p>

<p>Student-directed science documentaries include “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/growing-the-caribbean-glider-fleet/">Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet</a>,”  featuring scientists monitoring hurricane development; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/biting-back/">Biting Back: The Lifesaving Potential of Catnip</a>,” about the development of natural insect repellents; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/where-the-waters-meet-on-the-breathing-shore/">Where Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore</a>,” featuring climate scientists studying coastal ecosystems; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/the-b-a-s-i-l-project/">The B.A.S.I.L Project</a>,” about USDA-funded plant-breeding research; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/ocean-farming/">Ocean Farming</a>,” about NOAA supported oyster breeding; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/the-women-of-nsongwe/">The Women of Nsongwe</a>,” about USAID-supported agriculture projects in Zambia; and “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/skycatcher/">Skycatcher</a>,” about an NSF-funded atmospheric chemistry study in Alabama.</p>

<p>This science-in-action model offers a path forward that other universities could follow. Institutions can strengthen students’ STEM learning and science identities  while training a new generation of credible, relatable voices for science.</p>

When farmers’ fields are destroyed by an unknown pathogen, plant scientists spend years breeding new varieties of disease-resistant food crops
A team of microbiologists explore deep-sea volcanoes in search of organisms that may contain anticancer compounds
The science-in-action model teaches students to create documentaries that show the scientific research process
These are passionate people who are dedicated to seeking solutions to real-world problems
They are also the main characters in science documentaries produced in the Rutgers Immersive Learning Science Storytelling Lab that I oversee
Our lab pairs students with working scientists to co-create documentaries about research as it happens, while earning experiential learning credit
At a time when confidence in science is declining , I was approached by scientists who wanted their authentic research stories communicated to broad audiences
I am an educator, a researcher and anthropologist , and a science filmmaker who has been making science documentaries with Rutgers students and researchers since 2008
The science-in-action storytelling model I developed is intended to make the human journey of science visible to the public
Our stories communicate the process, motivations and integrity behind science, which helps earn public confidence and trust in science

I also partner with STEM learning researchers to gauge whether our documentaries increase the relatability of scientists, increase public understanding of scientific processes and help students find belonging in STEM
Our storytelling process Science-in-action storytelling is composed of five steps that support student-scientist relationships
First, the storytellers develop trust with the participating university scientists
This trust stems from shared respect and a mutual understanding of the co-creation process
The scientists then invite storytellers into their labs and field sites, where we capture their research processes in real time

Undergraduate philosophy major Ben Lerner was invited to accompany oceanographers to Barbados to make the documentary ‘Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet.’ Leah Hopson , CC BY Our professional storytelling team, which includes students, then documents scientists conducting research, including experiments and data collection, as they describe the why and how of their work
Depending on the complexity of the project, we collect dozens to hundreds of hours of science-in-action video footage
Importantly, this video data is maintained in our storytelling lab, as it often includes recordings of federally funded research
Maintaining the video data repository is a key component to establishing and sustaining trust with the participating scientists
Step 3 invites students to immerse themselves in the video data and begin shaping the footage into documentary scenes, constructed using only the scientists’ words, without narration
As they analyze hours of footage, our students learn about the authentic scientific processes; in doing so, they participate in research through the process of storytelling

Seidel , CC BY Our students are not graded on their documentary skills, nor are they required to make a film
Instead, they are graded on the science they learn through the storytelling process
Step 4 requires that the students share drafts of their documentary scenes with the featured scientist to verify the accuracy of the science communicated
This step is part of the foundational trust agreement with the scientists but is also an opportunity for the students to personally connect with scientists
For Step 5, our lab works to distribute the documentaries to a wide variety of audiences, including the general public
Here we partner with STEM learning experts to assess audiences’ understanding of and trust in the science communicated in the film and audience perceptions of the featured scientists

title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub
It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape
Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ
It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves

Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words
But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes
I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity
There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite

In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.  One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy
Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables)
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts

That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .  Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity
Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair

But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.  Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else
Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand

Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way
The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to
Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines
Companies also build diesel generators for backup
Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded
The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts
It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts
That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out)
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid

But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes
Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale
Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants
When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse

And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency)
Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around
Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do

But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers
Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think)
Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that

title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
excerpt: A new voice for AI regulation in Congress: Scott Wiener, who authored the country's first proposed frontier AI legislation, just won Nancy Pelosi's fo
body: A new voice for AI regulation in Congress: Scott Wiener, who authored the country's first proposed frontier AI legislation, just won Nancy Pelosi's former congressional seat and is already pushing for federal action — warning that "we could sleepwalk into a disaster." Recursive self-improvement is keeping him up at night: A recent report suggesting Anthropic may have achieved AI that meaningfully advances itself rattled Wiener, who sees it as proof that Congress is running out of time to act before losing control entirely

He wants regulation with real teeth: Wiener is pushing for a powerful federal AI regulator, whistleblower protections, kill switches, and auditing requirements — and he's firmly against federal laws that would strip states of their own ability to regulate

Cautious optimism, with caveats: Wiener is concerned about Congress's poor track record on tech regulation, wary of Trump's hostility to AI safety concerns, and hoping any crisis that forces action will be, as he puts it, "as small as possible." " data-chronoton-post-id="1148182" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI

Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.  I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor
But he was already thinking about AI risk

The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy

SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed

Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.  Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic

That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.  “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve

And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.  He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says

That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement
Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk
Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk
But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers

The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water

I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry

He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting
And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

body: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history

title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted

body: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994
High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party
